Health claims – Honduras

A 2012 Central American Technical Regulation (67.01.60:10) permits and regulates the use of nutrient function and disease risk reduction claims. Claims must be substantiated through information demonstrating the nutritional composition of the food, and the relationship between the claimed function of the food product and the beneficial effect on diet and health. The Ministry of Health has the responsibility to approve the use of claims on food containing high levels of nutrients that can increase risk of illness or health problems. Claims are not permitted on products that may promote or sanction excessive consumption of these nutrients or undermine good dietary practice. There are no generalised nutritional criteria that restrict their use on "unhealthy" food.

La Visión de País 2010-2038 recoge las condiciones de una nación posible y futura, materializada mediante el establecimiento de principios, cuatro grandes objetivos nacionales y 22 metas de prioridad nacional. Visión de País:
Objetivo 1: Una Honduras sin pobreza extrema, educada y sana, con sistemas consolidados de previsión social.
Objetivo 2: Una Honduras que se desarrolla en democracia, con seguridad y sin violencia.
Objetivo 3: Una Honduras productiva, generadora de oportunidades y empleo digno, que aprovecha de manera sostenible sus recursos y reduce la vulnerabilidad ambiental.
Objetivo 4: Un Estado moderno, transparente, responsable, eficiente y competitivo.

El documento comprende cinco capítulos, que integran los objetivos y resultados esperados, con carácter mandatorio para el periodo 2018-2021, e indicativo para 2022, para igual número de sectores: Bienestar y Desarrollo Social; Crecimiento Económico Incluyente y Sostenible; Infraestructura y Desarrollo Logístico; Sociedad más Justa, Pacifica e Inclusiva; y, Gobernabilidad Democrática y Desarrollo. Además, incluye un capítulo en el cual se abordan cuatro temas transversales: Promoción y Respeto de los Derechos Humanos; Seguridad Alimentaria y Nutricional; Protección y Conservación del Medio Ambiente; y, Desarrollo Territorial.

Asegurar que el pueblo hondureño tenga niveles de seguridad y convivencia, igual que los países del primer mundo, continuando con el combate a la criminalidad, en todas sus formas, y que nuestro pueblo viva sin miedo; con pleno respeto a los derechos humanos.
Terminar de reorganizar y fortalecer el Estado y sus instituciones, para que sea más eficiente, transparente y con servidores públicos, que tengan un compromiso de servicio hacia el pueblo. Seremos un país de orden, con reglas claras y con trámites simples.

Nutrient claims – Honduras

A 2012 Central American Technical Regulation (67.01.60:10) establishes rules on the use of specified nutrient content claims (ie levels of fat for a low-fat claim). Claims are not permitted on products that may promote or sanction excessive consumption of these nutrients or undermine good dietary practice. Although nutrition content claims need to meet certain criteria set out in the Regulation, there are no generalised nutritional criteria that restrict their use on "unhealthy" food.

La Política de Protección Social (PPS) busca generar, gradual y progresivamente, las condiciones sociales que contribuyan al bienestar personal y colectivo, así como a la potenciación de las habilidades y capacidades para el ejercicio pleno de los derechos que cada ciudadano tiene. Para ello, la PPS se aborda desde una visión integral, que contempla la articulación de tres componentes básicos: Prevención; Protección y Oportunidades y Competencias.

Objetivos específicos:
1.Reducir gradualmente la pobreza, la pobreza extrema, la vulnerabilidad y la exclusión social mediante la articulación de acciones estratégicas en materia de prevención, mitigación y superación de riesgos sociales, económicos y naturales.
2.Promover la protección social desde un enfoque integral e incluyente de acuerdo al ciclo de vida, a través de la interacción y articulación con la seguridad social, asistencia social, seguridad alimentaria, servicios de salud, educación, mercado laboral y otras políticas, programas y proyectos encaminados a la atención de la población sujeto de esta política.
3.Impulsar la articulación y el incremento de la oferta pública y privada de recursos, servicios y oportunidades del desarrollo social y económico, de manera eficaz y eficiente, para garantizar el bienestar y la vida digna de las personas, las familias y las comunidades sujetos de atención de esta política.
4.Fomentar la participación co-responsable de familias y comunidades, fortaleciendo su rol indelegable de protección y formación de sus integrantes, fomentando una cultura de derechos.
5.Apoyar de manera especial a grupos sociales que por razones relacionadas con su edad, género, multiculturalidad, discapacidad, orientación sexual e identidad de género, condición serológica o por carencia de protección se encuentran excluidos, en situación de alto riesgo social o presenten daños que requieren una atención especial.

Trans fat labeling – Hong Kong

In Hong Kong, in Nutrient lists on pre-packaged food must, by law, include the trans fat content of the food. The rules generally define how the trans fat content must be listed, and on what basis (eg per 100g/100ml or per serving). If the trans fat content falls below a certain threshold, it may be listed as 0g (eg less than 0.5g per serving, or less than 0.3g per 100g of food product).

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the EU provides export refunds for eggs. Council Regulation (EC) No 1234/2007 sets out the rules for providing the export refunds. This is due to the high input of raw material prices in the EU, which may cause the prices for certain farm products in the EU to be higher than the world price level for the same product. Export refunds are provided to exporters who must export their farmed goods to third countries, to bridge the gap between the EU price level and the world price level, to help them to better compete on world markets. The amount of the export refund can vary depending on the destination of the export. The values for the refunds must be fixed at least once every three months; however these can stay the same for longer than three months. The specific values can be found in the Commission Implementing Regulation mentioned in the comments.

Food-based dietary guidelines - Hungary

In 2004, Hungary published the 'Dietary guidelines for the adult population in Hungary' intended for all healthy adults. Hungary’s food guide is the ‘house of healthy nutrition’, which has cereals at the base and vegetables and fruits on the second level. The roof is made of animal source products (i.e. meats and dairy products). Foods from these groups should be part of the daily diet. Products high in sugar and fat should be eaten sparingly, and this is the reason why they are placed outside of the house.

Act XLVIII on Basic Requirements and Certain Restrictions of Commercial Advertising Activities

Based on Section 8 of Act XLVIII on Basic Requirements and Certain Restrictions of Commercial Advertising Activities (2008), Hungary prohibits all advertising directed at children under the age of 18 in child welfare and child protection institutions, kindergartens, elementary schools and their dormitories. Advertisements promoting a “healthy lifestyle” are exempt from the ban. The term “healthy lifestyle” is not defined by Section 8, and school boards determine on a case-by-case basis if an advertisement complies with this exception, in addition to adhering to national regulatory mechanisms and EU regulations on health claims. Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has established laws and regulations to govern the use and development of bio-technology. A major concern for the EU with regards to bio-technology is genetically modified organisms (GMOs), which is mainly regulated by Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003. The main objectives for these regulations are to protect human and animal health by introducing a safety assessment of the highest possible standards at EU level before any genetically modified (GM) food and feed is placed on the market; to have in place harmonised procedures for risk assessment and authorisation of GM food and feed that are efficient, time-limited and transparent; to ensure clear labelling of GM food and feed in order to respond to consumers’ concern and enable them to make an informed choice and to avoid misleading consumers; to set labelling requirements for GM feed which provide farmers with accurate information on the composition and properties of feed, thereby enabling them to make an informed choice. In order for GM food or feed to be allowed onto the European Market, it must go through an authorisation procedure. The first step in the procedure is the submission of an application for an authorisation for the placing on the market, which is followed by the preparation and the delivery of an opinion by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). The public is then allowed to make comments on the opinion, after which the European Commission prepares and adopts a decision.
EU legislation allows for countries within the EU to provisionally restrict or prohibit the use and/or sale of the GM product on its territory. Austria, France, Greece, Hungary, Germany, and Luxembourg have applied this safeguard measure to certain GM products within their territory.

Under the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), since the 2003 reform, the EU provides direct support to its farmers in the form of payments granted directly to them under certain support schemes. These include: the single payment scheme (SPS), the single area payment scheme (SAPS), and support schemes for farmers producing rice, starch potatoes, protein crops, nuts, seeds, cotton, sugar, fruit and vegetables, sheepmeat and goatmeal and veal and beef. Direct support of the EU is currently based on Council Regulation (EC) No 73/2009. The objective of the EU direct support is to provide a safety net for farmers in the form of a basic income as well as contribute to providing basic public goods delivered through sustainable farming. The budgetary ceilings for these direct support measures change every year. The yearly budget allocated by the EU is of around €40 billion.

The SPS entered into force in 2005 and is implemented by 17 countries of the EU, with the other 10 implementing the SAPS. 
The SAPS was offered as an option for countries joining the EU in 2004 and 2007 and will remain in force until 2013. It is a transition measure towards implementing the SPS. For the SAPS, the level of payment is calculated by dividing the country’s annual financial envelope by its respective utilized agricultural area. Under the SPS, support is granted in the form of a single annual payment dependent on the entitlement of the farmers. The three main options for calculating the value of payment entitlements include a historical, regional, and hybrid model. The historical model is based on the payments received by a farmer during a reference period, resulting in different aid levels per hectare. The regional model takes all payments received in a region and divides them by the number of eligible hectares, resulting in a flat rate. The hybrid model is made up of a mixture of the 2 other models. 
Cross-compliance ties the direct support for farmers with standards of environmental care, public/animal/plant health and animal welfare, penalising farmers who infringe EU law by reducing the support they receive. Cross-compliance covers directives and regulations which formulate “statutory management requirements”, which apply to all farmers, even if they are not receiving direct support from the EU. In order to help farmers better understand and meet the EU rules set up by cross compliance, every member state has established a Farm Advisory System. 

In addition to this, the EU established a set of rules on good agricultural and environmental conditions which farmers must comply with in order to receive payments under the CAP. 

The CAP reform in 2003 decoupled direct support to farmers, so that payments were no longer linked to production of a specific product. Up to 10% of the budget allocated for each Member states, is made available to support specific sectors for the purposes of: 
1) Protecting or enhancing the environment
2) Improving the quality of agricultural products,
3) Improving the marketing of agricultural products,
4) Practicing enhanced animal welfare standards,
5) Specific agricultural activities entailing additional agro-environment benefits
6) Payments for disadvantages affecting farmers in specific sectors (dairy, beef, veal, sheep and goat and rice) in economically or environmentally sensitive areas as well as for economically vulnerable types of farming,
7) Top-ups to existing Single Payment Scheme payment entitlements in areas where land abandonment is a threat
8) Support for risk assurance in the form of contributions to crop, animal and plant insurance premia
9) Support by way of mutual funds for animal and plant diseases and environmental incidents.

From 2012 at the latest, all of these coupled payments will be decoupled and integrated into the SPS, except for the suckler cows, sheep and goat and cotton schemes which may remain linked to the production of those products.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) regulates animal health and welfare. This is based upon Article 13 of the Treaty of the Functioning of the European Union which recognises animals as sentient beings and requires full regard to be given to the welfare requirements of animals. Council Directive 2002/99/EC is the main legislation with regards to animal health and welfare. Countries within the EU may choose to implement stricter regulations, providing that they are compatible with those set out in the Treaty. The regulations cover the protection of animals during transport, at the time of slaughter and killing, protection of animals for scientific and experimental purposes, and the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. The principle which EU law with regards to animal welfare is based upon include freedom from discomfort, hunger, thirst, fear, distress, pain, injury, disease, and the freedom to express natural behaviour. 
This Animal Health Strategy has 4 main objectives of ensuring a high level of public health and food safety, supporting farming and the rural economy, improving economic growth/cohesion/competitiveness, and to promote farming practices and animal welfare which prevent animal health related threats and minimise environmental impacts.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has been regulating plant health and variety. The main legislation with regards to plant health and variety is Council Directive 2000/29/EC (amending Council Directive 77/93/EEC).
The main objective of EU plant health legislation is to protect the safety of food derived from plants and to secure the health and quality status of crops in the EU. The legislation regulates the trade of plants and plant products within the EU as well as imports from the rest of the world in accordance with international plant health standards and obligations. This is partially done through providing protective measures against the spread of harmful organisms. The legislation contains a list of harmful organisms that threaten plant health in the EU. This includes the establishment of the European Union Notification System for Plant Health Interceptions (EUROPHYT), which is a rapid alert system dealing with interceptions for plant health reasons of plants and plant products imported into the EU or being traded within the EU itself. EUROPHYT also contributes to the implementation of preventative measures by ensuring that the data on risks to plant and plant products is up-to-date and accurate. 
The legislation with regards to plant health is known as the Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR). The Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR) looks towards contributing to sustainable production through plant health protection; ensuring competitiveness of the agriculture complex; contribute to the protection of public and private green, forests, and the landscape, and to ensure food security. 
The selling and use of plant protection products and their residue in food is also regulated.  Council Directive 91/414/EEC is concerned with the placing of plant protection products on the market. No plant protection product may be used within the EU unless it has been scientifically established that the products have no harmful effects on consumers, farmers, and local residents and passers-by; they do not cause unacceptable effects on the environment; and that they are sufficiently effective against pests. 
Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 currently governs the maximum residue levels (MRLs) of pesticides in food and feed in order to protect the health of consumers. These are controlled by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). If any infringements of the Regulation are found, these shall be countered by sanctions of the product.

The Farm-to-Fork Strategy has been developed by the European Union to accelerate its transition to a sustainable food system. The Strategy sets ambitious targets:

a reduction by 50% of the sales of antimicrobials for farmed animals and in aquaculture by 2030
and reaching 25% of agricultural land under organic farming by 2030
Finally, the strategy also includes the aim for all rural areas to have access to fast broadband by 2025, to enable digital innovation.

EU health claims – Hungary 

Regulation 1924/2006 (applicable as of July 2007) establishes EU-wide rules on the use of health claims (claims on nutrient function, disease risk reduction and children's health). Companies may only use health claims that are substantiated and authorised by the European Commission and Member States (various regulations authorising health claims to date). The European Food Safety Authority is responsible for verifying the scientific substantiation of claims; it has done so for claims currently in use and continues to do so for claims that are proposed and applied for by companies that want to use health claims in the EU. In theory, health claims may only be used on food defined as "healthy" by a nutrient profile. This nutrient profiling restriction was due to be implemented in 2010 but no model has yet been established. Therefore, permitted health claims can be used as long as the conditions for use of the claim as set out in the respective regulations are met. Once nutrient profiles are established, health claims may only be used on food products deemed "healthy".

EU nutrient claims – Iceland

Regulation 1924/2006 establishes EU-wide rules on the use of specified nutrient content and comparative claims (ie levels of fat for a low-fat claim). This Regulation is also applicable in Iceland as a member of the European Economic Area. As of January 2010, only nutrition claims as listed in the Regulation’s annex are permitted. In theory, these nutrition claims may only be used on food defined as "healthy" by a nutrient profile. This nutrient profiling restriction was due to be implemented in 2010 but no model has yet been established. Therefore, permitted nutrition claims can be used as long as the conditions for use of the claim as set out in the annex are met. Once nutrient profiles are established, nutrition claims may only be used on food products deemed "healthy", though two notable exceptions will apply: nutrition claims referring to the reduction of fat, saturated fats, trans fats, sugars and salt/sodium will be allowed without reference to a profile for the specific nutrient, provided the claims comply with the conditions of the Regulation; and a nutrition claim may be used even if a single nutrient exceeds the nutrient profile as long as a statement in relation to this nutrient appears on the label in close proximity to, on the same side and with the same prominence, as the claim (the statement must read: 'High [name of nutrient] content').

Food–based dietary guidelines – India

In 2011, India published revised 'Dietary guidelines for Indians - a manual' directed at the general public including recommendations for different population groups. India uses a number of graphical elements to represent the messages of its guidelines, one of them being a food pyramid. The pyramid is divided into four levels of foods according to recommended consumption: cereals and legumes/beans at the base should be eaten in sufficient quantity, vegetables and fruits on the second level should be eaten liberally, animal source foods and oils on the third level are to be eaten moderately, and at the apex, highly processed foods high in sugar and fat to be eaten sparingly.

The National Environment Policy, 2006 is the outcome of extensive consultations with experts in different disciplines, Central Ministries, Members of Parliament, State Governments, Industry Associations, Academic and Research Institutions, Civil Society, NGOs and the Public. The policy also seeks to stimulate partnerships of different stakeholders, i.e. public agencies, local communities, academic and scientific institutions, the investment community, and international development partners, in harnessing their respective resources and strengths for environmental management.

The priorities set in the Strategy for Doubling Farmers Income by 2022 represent the key overarching framework for the agriculture sector. The main objective of the government is to double farmers’ income by solving the twin problems of maximising efficiency and ensuring equity in a sustainable manner. These objectives will be met through diversification into high value fruits and vegetables, increased participation of private players, improved agriculture marketing at state levels, and policy reforms related to leasing. The government is also focussing on boosting productivity through increased adoption of scientifically proven and sustainable agriculture practices such as introduction of improved varieties, integrated soil management, promotion of organic farming and efficient water management practices.
An Inter-ministeral Committee was set up to implement the Strategy. The Committee has identified seven sources of income growth namely, improvement in crop productivity; improvement in livestock productivity; resource use efficiency or savings in the cost of production; increase in the cropping intensity; diversification towards high value crops; improvement in real prices received by farmers; and shift from farm to non-farm occupations. However, the discussion on new programs and initiatives to effective implementation of the strategy is still being under discussion.

Higher prices will support production and boost stocking through assured remunerative prices to the farmers.

The National Dairy Development Board has created a “National Dairy Plan” (NDP) in order to increase Indian milk production by 6 million tonnes annually over the next 15 years. The first phase of the plan (financial outlay of USD 416 million) will have an implementation period of 6 years and has the aim to increase dairy production through improved breeding and feeding practices as well as improved extension and management services. It will also emphasize expansion of India’s dairy cooperatives.

According to Oryza, the government will start supplying subsidized foodgrains in 5-kilo packs under the Public Distribution System (PDS), thus replacing the existing system of distribution in 50-kilo bags to PDS outlets which then sell rice in loose. The objective is to prevent corruption in the implementation of the Food Security Law and to help control soaring rice prices in the country. The government will pilot the new type of distribution via PDS outlets in Punjab and Andhra Pradesh, the India’s two major rice producing states (Oryza, 06 November 2013).

The  Government has got a study done on “Assessment of Quantitative Harvest and Post-Harvest Losses of Major Crops and Commodities in India” by ICAR - Central Institute of Post-Harvest Engineering and Technology (CIPHET), Ludhiana.The study has estimated that annual value of harvest and post-harvest losses of major agricultural produces at national level was of the order of Rs. 92,651 crore calculated using production data of 2012-13 at 2014 wholesale prices.
Ban on onion exports revoked following farmers protest, but the previous minimum export price (MEP) set at USD 475/tonne is retained.

The export of wheat and non-basmati rice is allowed also to state-run trading companies. Minimum export price (MEP) for Basmati rice lowered  by 22 percent to USD 700 per tonne, from USD 900 per tonne, to stimulate exports.

The Ministry of State for Agriculture and Food Processing Industries launched the Investors’ Portal for Food Processing Industry to provide information - particularly to investors - on infrastructure facilities for food processing units, availability of raw material, marketing infrastructure and fiscal incentives in a user friendly mode and help them to make informed decisions (Press Information Bureau, 15 October 2013).

The Union Cabinet has approved a long-term contract by signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Mozambique for import of pulses either through the private channels or Government-to-Government (G2G) sales through State Agencies nominated by the two countries. The MoU aims at promoting the production of Pigeon Peas/Tur and other pulses in Mozambique by encouraging progressive increase in the trading of these pulses. The MOU includes targets for exports of Tur and other pulses from Mozambique to India for five financial years and aims at doubling the trade from 100 000 tonnes in 2016-17 to 200 000 tonnes is 2020-21. The MoU will augment domestic availability of pulses in India and thereby stabilise its prices.

The Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution revised the raw sugar subsidy of INR 3 371 per tonne from August 1, 2014, to September 30, 2014. In February 2014, the Indian Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs decided that over four million metric tons (MMT) of raw sugar would be eligible to receive subsidies over the next two years.

The governemnt of India issued the Draft National Forest Policy, 2018. The overall objective and goal of the present policy is to safegard the ecological and livelihood security of people, of the present and future generations, based on sustainable management of the forests for the flow of ecosystem services in order.

The Conference of States’ Food Ministers agreed to develop and implement an action plan for the next six months for maintaining adequate supplies of select essential commodities at reasonable prices and to ensure that market interventions are made on a real-time basis. The Plan will cover will cover rice, onions, tomatoes, potatoes, edible oils, bread, milk and eggs, among others and include: Mapping of vulnerable areas  prone to supply shortages for special monitoring; Mobilization of existing storage capacity utilizing the  Government/private/cooperative storage infrastructure to ensure adequate  decentralized stocks; establishment of a Price Monitoring Cell to monitor prices (wholesale and retail from various  parts of the State); Take effective measures against hoarders and Black-marketers. States also recommended the government to set up a “Price Stabilisation Fund” to enable them to undertake market intervention to tackle rise in food prices, and amend the Essential Commodities Act to make it more stringent (PIB, 04 July 2014).

On 14 April 2014, the government announced plans to expand farmland under irrigation by at least 10 percent over the next three years, to around 107 million ha, in an attempt to boost grains output and to reduce dependency on monsoon rains (IGC, 25 April 2014).
Allocation of 2 million tons of wheat from its stocks for "humanitarian" exports in MY 2008/09 for neighboring countries.
Export tax abolished for basmati rice.

The Government of India decided to revise the buffer norms for rice and wheat in the Central Pool (food grains stocks procured by Central Government and State Governments through minimum support price operations), which remained unchanged since 2005.

India signed a Mou with the BRICS in energy saving and energy efficiency. The MoU provides the following areas of cooperation in the field of Energy Savings and Energy Efficiency: Joint scientific and technological research, conferencing and holding of lectures and seminars; capacity building and technology transfer; technology development, sharing policies and best practices; encouragement of use of energy efficient and energy saving approaches and instruments in the work of the business entities of the BRICS countries, carried out within the BRICS countries in Consultation with the host country.

India’s National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) outlines existing and future policies and programmes directed at climate change mitigation and adaptation. These National Missions will be institutionalized by respective ministries and will be organised through inter-sectoral groups that include, in addition to related Ministries, the Ministry of Finance and the Planning Commission, experts from industry, acade¬mia and civil society. The institutional structure will vary depending on the task to be addressed and will include the opportunity to compete on the best management model.

Additional 500 000 tonnes of sugar exports permitted under the open general license (OGL) for the current 2010-11 marketing season (October-September). This is over and above the already permitted 1 million tonnes, cleared through two equal installments on April 19 and June 28.

Creation of the National Rain fed Areas Authority (NRAA) to work in coordination with the Planning Commission to boost watershed development. The new initiative orientates policies through a set of guidelines: (i) delegating powers to states; (ii) dedicated implementing agencies with multidisciplinary teams at national, state and district level; (iii) duration and phasing of programmes from 4 to 7 years; and (iv) livelihood orientation.
Fertilizer subsidy as a ratio to the value of crop output risen to more than 10 per cent in 2008-09 due to a spike in the price of imported fertilizers.
Scheduled tribes and other traditional forest Dwellers. Recognition of forest rights.
Tariff-rate-quota imposed on corn imports, subject to an in-quota tariff of 15 percent; above- quota imports face a 50 percent duty.

To curb the losses in supply chain of agriculture produce and to improve the existing infrastructure for food processing, the Ministry of Food Processing Industries has been implementing the Schemes of:
- Mega Food Parks: provides modern Infrastructure for food processing units in the country on pre-identified cluster basis. Under the scheme, grant-in-aid is provided at 50 percent of the eligible project cost in general areas and 75 percent thereof in difficult areas and hilly areas, subject to a maximum of Rs.50.00 Crore per project.  A total of 42 Mega Food Park projects have been approved by the Government to be set up in the country.
- The Scheme of Cold Chain, Value Addition and Preservation Infrastructure aims at arresting post-harvest losses of horticulture & non-horticulture produce and providing remunerative price to farmers for their produce. Under the scheme, financial assistance is provided in the form of grant-in-aid of maximum Rs.10 Crore per project for setting up of integrated cold chain and preservation infrastructure facilities without any break from the farm gate to the consumer. The scheme is available in all States/UTs and rural & urban areas. So far, 134 Integrated Cold Chain Projects have been sanctioned by the Ministry in the country to reduce the cold chain gap. Of this, 88 Integrated Cold Chain projects have achieved completion and commenced commercial operation, 46 Integrated Cold Chain projects are in various stages of implementation.
- Setting up/ Modernization of Abattoirs. aims to provide hygienic finished meat and meat products, slaughter waste management and pollution control. The Scheme envisaged grant-in-aid at 50 percent of the project cost in general areas and 75 percent for North- Eastern region subject to a maximum of Rs.15.00 Crore per project. So far, 41 Abattoir projects have been sanctioned.
Export ban on pulses extended untill March 2013. However, exports of garbanzo beans and 10 000 tonnes of organic pulses are exempted from the ban.
On 3 March 2010, the Commerce Secretary permitted the export of 45,000 tons non-basmati rice to Nepal and Sri Lanka.

The Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) Act (1976) was amended to enhance authorized and issued capital to strengthen their capital base. This modification intends to ensure financial stability of RRBs and to meet credit demand of rural areas (Press Information Bureau, 31 January 2013).
The Government lower the duty on wheat imports by the private traders to 5 percent from 50 percent, effective from June 28, 2006.

Technology Mission on Oilseeds, Pulses & Maize launched in 1986 (pulses, oil palm and maize were brought within the purview of the Mission in 1990-91) intends to promote crop diversification, increase production and offer a flexible implementation scheme for states. The specific objectives of the integrated approach are to step-up production through scientific handling of harvest, procurement, storage care and efficient scientific processing with a view to achieving the qualitative and quantitative ultimate product.
Minimum support price of wheat increased by 1.8 percent to INR 11 200 (USD 252) per tonne, for the 2011/2012 marketing year (April/March).

The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has approved the export of 2 million tonnes of wheat from the Central Pool stock during the current financial year subject to a floor price of USD 300 per tonne through the Central Public Sector to be completed by 31 March 2014 (Press Information Bureau, 08 August 2013).

The Department of Fertilizers has notified a New Investment Policy - 2012  to encourage investment in the urea sector and accomplish self-sufficiency in urea by end of 12th Five Year Plan (2012-17) (Press Information Bureau, 08 January 2013).

Increase on the amount of agriculture credit disbursed by Kisan Credit Card Scheme. This scheme was formulated in 1998-99 on the basis of the farmer's land holdings, for uniform adoption by banks, so that the farmers may use them to readily purchase agricultural inputs such as seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, etc. and also draw cash for their production needs.

In order to take part in this global programme of REDD+, India develops the National REDD+ Strategy or Action Plans on reducing emissions from deforestation, forest degradation and fulfilling the role of conservation of forest carbon stocks and sustainable management of forests. The Strategy builds upon existing national circumstances and in line with India’s National Action Plan on Climate Change, Green India Mission and India’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). 
The overarching objective of National REDD+ Strategy (NRPS) of India is to facilitate implementation of REDD+ programme in the country in conformity with relevant decisions of UNFCCC, in particular the Cancun. REDD+ activities are defined and implemented in three phases: (i) Phase 1 is the development of national strategies or action plans, policies and measures, and capacity-building; (ii) Phase 2 is the implementation of national policies and measures and national strategies or action plans that could involve further capacity-building, technology development and transfer and results-based demonstration activities; (iii) Phase 3 is the evolvement into results based actions that should be fully measured, reported and verified. The strategy will follow the sub-national approach to implement the Sub-national REDD+ Action Plans. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change will coordinate relevant agencies in developing and implementing appropriate policies, methodologies, procedures and technologies relating to REDD+ implementation in the country.

The Hydro-meteorological Data Dissemination Policy (2013) provides for hosting of all unclassified data (after validation and to the extent published in Water Year Book, Water Quality Year Book, Water Sediment Year Book, Ground Water Year Book) on IndiaWRIS (web based Water Resources Information System) website, which can be downloaded by any web-registered user free of cost.

COVID-19: The Union Cabinet chaired by the Prime Minister has approved further extension of Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY) as part of Economic Response to COVID-19 for additional allocation of food-grains from the Central Pool for another five months from July to November, 2020. The PMGKAY psrovides additional free-of-cost foodgrains at the scale of 5 Kg per person per month to the poor, so that poor and vulnerable families/beneficiaries are able to access food-grains easily without facing any financial distress. Under this programme initially, free food-grains for three months i.e. April, May and June were provided.

National Action Plan for Children, 2016 (NPAC) was launched at a special function held to celebrate the National Girl Child Day in New Delhi. The NPAC has been developed by the Ministry of Women & Child Development. The Action Plan has four key priority areas; survival, health and nutrition; education and development; protection and participation. The NPAC  defines objectives, sub-objectives, strategies , action points and indicators for measuring progress under the four key priority areas and also identifies key stakeholders for the implementation of different strategies. The plan also puts focus on new and emerging concerns for children such as online child abuse, children affected by  natural and man-made disasters and climate change, etc. The strategies and action points largely draw upon the existing programmes and schemes of various Ministries/Departments. However, for new and emerging issues related to children; it also suggests formulation of new programmes and strategies, as required. The plan takes into account the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and provides a roadmap towards achieving them though co-ordination and convergence with different stakeholders.

The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (Prime Minister's Crop Insurance Scheme) was launched by Prime Minister of India Narendra Modi on 18 February 2016. It incorporates the best features of all previous schemes and at the same time, all previous shortcomings / weaknesses have been removed. The PMFBY will replace the existing two schemes National Agricultural Insurance Scheme as well as the Modified NAIS.  The Scheme can cover all the Crops for which past yield data is available
and grown during the notified season, in a Notified Area and for which yield estimation at the Notified Area level will be available based on requisite number of Crop Cutting Experiments (CCEs) being a part of the General Crop Estimation Survey (GCES).

A new scheme, the National Project on Management of Soil Health & Fertility (NPMSF), has been introduced in 2008-09 with a view to setting up of 500 new Soil Testing Laboratories (STLs) and 250 Mobile Soil Testing Laboratories (MSTLs) and strengthening of the existing State STLs for micronutrient analysis.

A Financing Agreement for IDA credit of US$ 50 million (equivalent) for the “Nai Manzil- Education and Skills Training for Minorities” was signed here with the World Bank.
The project takes an integrated and holistic approach towards education and skill development of the minority youth, to address the high dropout and unemployment rate among them. Improvement in the education attainment of the minority youth in the project area and improvement in their employability skills are among the expected outcomes of the project.

In view of existing stock position of food grains in the Central Pool, the Centre has decided to permit the states/UTs for lifting and distributing six months quota of food grains in one go, under the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) (Press Information Bureau, 24 and 28 May 2012).
The import duty on sugarcane decreased from 7.5 percent to 2.5 percent.

Through the Scheme for Cold Chain, Value Addition and Preservation Infrastructure, the Ministry of Food Processing Industries provides financial assistance to strengthen the cold chain infrastructure and provide infrastructural facilities like sorting, packaging and processing horticulture products, by partially covering plant, machinery and technical works costs (subject to a maximum of INR 100 billion ~ USD 1.8 billion).

the government of India issued the Guidelines on Access to Biological Resources and Associated Knowledge and Benefits Sharing Regulations, 2014, which implements the Biological Diversity Act 2002. It was made  in pursuance of the Nagoya Protocol on access to genetic resources and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their utilization to the Convention on Biological Diversity. It consists of 15 parts, making regulations on procedure for access to biological resources and/ or associated traditional knowledge for research or bio-survey and bio-utilization for research, procedure for access to biological resources, for commercial utilization or for bio-survey and bio-utilization for commercial utilization and etc.
Wheat and rice to be sold through ration shops at a price of INR 8.42 (USD 0.18) and INR 11.82 (USD 0.25) per kilogram, respectively. These prices are lower than the minimum support prices.
Exemption from the 10 percent import duty for pulses.

Removal of the 70% import tax on certain varieties of rice in an effort to boost supplies, after late and uneven monsoon rains led to a significant reduction in summer-sown main (Kharif) crop planting. Duty-free imports of semi and wholly milled rice will now be permitted until 30 September 2010.

On 12 February 2014, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) agreed on an export subsidy on raw sugar of INR 3 333 (US$ 53.52) per tonnes, to be reviewed every two months based on international sugar prices and currency exchange rates. The subsidy is to infuse capital into the sugar industry, make the commodity more competitive on a global scale, and help millers clear their debts with farmers (USDA, 14 February 2014).

On 26 December 2013, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approved the proposal to provide interest subvention for financial assistance to the sugar industry for effecting cane price payments. The Central Government will provide an interest subvention up to 12 percent for the additional working capital loans to the sugar undertakings provided by the banks. The scheme is financed by the Sugar Development Fund (Press Information Bureau, 26 December 2013).

Development and Strengthening of Infrastructure Facilities for Production and distribution of Quality Seeds Scheme. Its objective is to distribute seeds at 50 percent of the cost. During 2008-09 more than 25,000 seed villages were organized across the country; certified quality seed production increased  from 194.31 to 250.35 lakh.

On March 7, 2013, the Group of Ministers approved the exports of 5.0 million tonnes of government-held wheat from Punjab and Haryana by private traders, through bidding process for the allocation with the floor price set at INR 14,800 (USD 274) per tonne.

In November 2016, entire country got National Food Security Act coverage. As a result, now 81.34 crore persons will get wheat at Rs. 2/ kg and rice at Rs. 3/ kg. Being an important initiative for ensuring food security of the people, the Government of India actively pursued with all the States/UTs for its early implementation. At this current coverage, monthly allocation of foodgrains to States/UTs under the Act is about 45.5 lakh tons, with subsidy implication of about Rs. 11,726 core per month or about Rs. 1,40, 700 crore per year.

Following recommendations by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices for the Rabi marketing season 2013/14, the government agreed to release wheat stocks from time to time through Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) and/or Open Market Sale Scheme (OMSS), with the aim of stabilizing prices  (Press Information Bureau, 10 December 2012).

The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has approved the proposal for increasing the import duty on refined edible oils of vegetable origin from 7.5 to 10 percent, in order to protect the domestic refining industry and domestic farmers. Similarly, to protect the interest of rubber growers, the basic customs duty on natural rubber has been increased from 20 percent or INR 20 per kg, whichever is lower, to 20 percent or INR 30 per kg, whichever is lower. (Press Information Bureau, 09 and 21 December 2013).

The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) approved the continuation of the same scale of food grains allocation totaling 4.189 million tonnes of wheat and 1.984 million tonnes of rice, to be distributed to Above the Poverty Line (APL) families during 2013-14 under the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS). This will assure a minimum allocation of 15 kg per household per month in 22 States/UTs and 35 kg per household per month in other 13 States/UTs (News Bureau 16 May 2013)

Livestock Insurance Scheme implemented as a regular scheme in the 100 newly selected districts from 2008/09 till the end of 11th Five Year Plan. It intends to (i) provide protection mechanism to the farmers and cattle rearers against any eventual loss of their animals due to death and to demonstrate the benefit of the insurance of livestock to the people and (ii) popularize it with the ultimate goal of attaining qualitative improvement in livestock and their products. The scheme covers crossbred and high yielding cattle and buffaloes are being insured at maximum of their current market price. The premium of the insurance is subsidized to the tune of 50%. The entire cost of the subsidy is being borne by the Central Government. The benefit of subsidy is being provided to a maximum of 2 animals per beneficiary for a policy of maximum of three years. The scheme is being implemented in all states except Goa through the State Livestock Development Boards of respective states.

The Ministry of Water Resources formulated a “model bill” to regulate and control groundwater development, management and protection from contamination. A Water Quality Assessment Authority (WQAA) was also constituted to monitor and report on ground water and surface water pollution (Press Information Bureau, 14 March 2013).

National Scheme of Welfare of Fishermen - Accident Insurance for Active Fishermen  for Rs.$50,000/- against death or permanent total disability and Rs.$25,000/- for partial permanent disability. The insurance cover will be for a period of 12 months and a policy would be taken out by FISHCOPFED in respect of all the participating States/ UT’s. The annual premium payable would not exceed Rs.$15/- per head – 50% of which will be subsidized as grants-in-aid by the Centre and the remaining 50% by the State Government. In the case of Union Territories, 100% premium will be borne by the Central Government.

Release of 2.5 million tonnes of wheat and rice  from the federal reserve stocks to be sold to poor families Below Poverty Line (BPL). Wheat will be sold at INR 4.15 (USD 0.092) per kilogram and rice at INR 5.65 (USD 0.13) per kilogram, significantly lower than market prices. In addition, 2.5 million tonnes of wheat and rice will be released and sold to poor families Above Poverty Line (APL) at INR 11.85 (USD 0.26) and INR 8.45 (USD 0.19) per kilogram repectively.

New initiatives have been proposed in the 12th Five Year Plan for retaining youth in Agriculture Sector and funding for research and innovations in the sector. The twin objectives of the plan are ensuring food security and improving the lot of farmers through higher investments in agriculture and allied sectors.
A subsidies programme to support the integrated use of  fertilizers  has been approved. Before, subsidies were given only on urea, making it cheaply available and endemically overused.
inistry of Water Resources has evolved the National Water Policy (2012) to meet the present challenges in the water sector.

Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) to increase the minimum support price (MSP) for common paddy during the 2015/16 kharif marketing season (October September) by about Rs.50 per quintal (around $7.8 per ton) or about 3.6% to around Rs.1,410 per quintal (around $220 per ton), according to local sources.

The Indian government decided to merge various public agriculture insurance schemes into the National Crop Insurance Program (NCIP) effective since 1 November 2013 and it allowed private sector companies to enter the agriculture insurance market. Private insurers with adequate infrastructure and experience will be authorized to implement NCIP besides the Agriculture Insurance Company of India (AIC) in order to provide better alternatives and services to farmers. According to the new regulations, loanee farmers will be covered on compulsory basis under the NCIP, while non-loanee farmers can choose either the Modified National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (MNAIS) or the Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme (WBCIS) components of the scheme (Ministry of Agriculture, 1 November 2013).

India has approved the increase of Minimun Support Prices for summer (Kharif) 2015/16 crops. The increase in MSPs which would be effective from the beginning of October will be applicable for various crops including rice, maize and soyabeans.

Intensive Cotton Development Programme (ICDP) aims to enhance the production, per unit area  through (a) technology transfer, (b) supply of quality seeds, (c) elevating IPM activities/ and (d) providing adequate and timely supply of  inputs to the farmers.

Introduction of a nutrient-based subsidy regime wherein the subsidy of fertilizers, other than urea, will remain fixed based on the nutrient composition and the retail prices of fertilizers will be decided by the manufacturers/importers.
Extension of the Technology Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture in North East (TMNE) to other three states in addition to NE states making it operational in 11 states.

Price stabilization fund scheme (PSF) announced a price spectrum band for the year 2004 for tea, coffee and rubber. The annual average domestic price during 2004 was Rs 62.42/ tea kg, Rs 72.16/ coffee- Arabica kg, Rs 34.93/ coffee- Robusta kg, and Rs 55.71/ rubber kg.

COVID-19:  The Government has decided to take steps to incentivize private investment in start-ups post the COVID-19 pandemic with certain measures in terms of tax, regulatory and RBI led monetary relief.

National Horticulture Mission (NHM) was launched in 2005-06 with the objective to provide holistic growth of agriculture sector adopting end to end approach involving production, post harvest management, processing marketing, capacity building and human resource development. 

Budget allocated:  Rs. 1100 crore.

The National Agroforestry Policy, which deals with the practice of integrating trees, crops and livestock on the same plot of land, was launched February 10, the first day of the World Congress on Agroforestry, held in Delhi. The policy, approved by the Cabinet on February 6, deals with problems agroforestry sector is facing at present, including adverse policies, weak markets and a dearth of institutional finance. Agroforestry has the potential to achieve sustainability in agriculture while optimising its productivity and mitigating climate change impact.

On 14 June 2019, Government of India has notified to prepare the “National Mariculture Policy 2019” which provides guidance for promoting 'Blue Growth Initiative' which focus on ushering 'Blue Revolution' by sustainable utilization of fisheries wealth from the marine and other aquatic resources of the country for improving the lives and livelihoods of fishermen and their families. 
The goal of the policy is to ensure sustainable farmed seafood production for the benefit of food and nutritional security and safeguard of the nation and to provide additional livelihood and entrepreneurial opportunities. The specific objectives of the policy are: 
-	To enhance mariculture production in India and increase incomes and employment opportunities in a sustainable manner.
-	To promote entrepreneurship in mariculture by facilitating the technical and financial inputs 
-	To adopt an environmentally sustainable approach for development of mariculture.

Under the 2013-14 Union Budget (April-March), the Government announced the allocation of  INR 132.15 billion (USD 2.43 billion) for a mid-day meal program for school children and INR 177 billion (USD 3.25 billion) for an Integrated Child Development Service and other programmes to promote protein rich foods. Several state governments are also promoting increased utilization of low-cost high-protein supplements derived from soybeans (Ministry of Finance, 28 February 2013)..

Import ban extended on specified live animals and livestock products from countries with outbreaks of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) and Low Pathogenic Avian Influenza (LPAI), for six more months.

The Ministry of Environment and Forests (MoEF) has released the draft of India’s new National Forest Policy (NFP), proposing the levy of a green tax. It has also touched upon the contentious issue of human-animal conflict. This draft National Forest Policy will replace the one crafted in 1988. Incorporating consequences of climate change but entirely ignoring one of the three forest related laws, the Forest Rights Act, the policy brings new focus to plantations, growing trees outside forest lands and wood industry. The policy continues with the national goal of a minimum of one-third of the geographical area under forest or tree cover.

COVID-19: 14 July 2020 – Indian Railways authority creates post COVID-19 coach. Indian Railways’ production unit, Rail Coach Factory, Kapurthala, has developed a Post Covid Coach to fight the COVID-19. This coach has design improvements in the coach like handsfree amenities, copper-coated handrails & latches, plasma air purification and titanium dioxide coating for COVID free passenger journey.

On April 18th, 2013 the Union Cabinet approved the National Policy for Children to help in the implementation of programmes and schemes for children all over the country. The policy gives utmost priority to right to life, health and nutrition and also gives importance to development, education, protection and participation.
