Release of additional 457 000 tonnes of  grains (182 000 tonnes of rice and 274 000 tonnes of wheat) to be sold at a subsidized price to poor families Above Poverty Line (ABP). Since May 2010, the Government has allocated more than 3 million tonnes of food grain to target poor families.

Approval to leverage the current bilateral trade of the Common Market of Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) to a Free Trade Agreement.  The Trade and Economic Relations Committee held its 17th meeting on the 29th April 2011 under the chairmanship of the Prime Minister .

Minikit Programme for Rice, Wheat & Coarse Cereals. The objective is to increase the productivity by popularizing the use of newly released hybrid/high yielding varieties and spread the area coverage under location specific high yielding varieties/hybrids.

Bulog Regional Divisions started the distribution of subsidized rice to targeted household through the RASKIN programme in different areas of the country. Bulog rice stocks is secured until September 2013 (Bulog, 10 February 2013).

New regulations (No. 27/permentan/PP.340/5/2009 in May 2009 and No. 38/Permentan/PP.340/8/2009 in August 2009) for the food safety control on imported and exported fresh food of plant origin (FFPO). Involved products: include barley, wheat, oats, rice, maize, rye and sorghum.

The government allocated IDR 40 billion (USD 4.1 million) for farmers whose land has been affected by natural disasters Serang, Banten. This financial compensation is intended to be invested in new seeds and to improve management of rice fields (Ministry of Agriculture, 7 November 2012).

Indonesia launched the Master Strategy of Agricultural Development in Indonesia in 2013-2045 in 2013. Its primary objective is to build sustainable agriculture-bioindustry. The strategy is based on spatial planning and agrarian reform; integrated tropical farming systems; economic activities of production, information and technology; post-harvest, agro-based rural energy and bioindustry; marketing system and product value chain; agricultural financing system; system research, innovation and quality human resources; infrastructure of agriculture and rural legislation, regulation and management.

Implementation of the second phase of ASEAN – China Free Trade Agreement (ACFTA) signed by Indonesia in November 2002. 
The ACFTA required Indonesia to reduce or eliminate the import duties in three phases for three categories. 
The Early Harvest Program (EHP), which began on January 1, 2004, gradually reduced to zero import duties by 2006. Agricultural commodities in this category include live animals, meat and meat products, fish, milk products, other animal based products, live trees, vegetables, fruits, and nuts. 
The second phase, which started in July 20, 2005, gradually reduced to zero import duty by January 1, 2010 for commodities included in Normal Track 1 (NT1) and by January 2012 for commodities included in NT2 products. The last phase is the reduction and elimination of import duties for Sensitive Track (ST) and Highly Sensitive Track (HST). For products under the HST category, the reduction of duties (0-20 percent) will commence in 2012 to become fully implemented in 2018.
Under ACFTA, Indonesia can export its wheat flour to ASEAN countries with zero percent duty and to China with 35 percent import duty. While wheat flour industry in China can export its products to Indonesia under the 5 percent Most Favored Nations (MFN) duty.

The current national spatial plan, which was established as National Spatial Plan (Law No. 26/2008), covers 20-year period and it is to be reviewed every five years. The organization responsible for drafting the plan was the National Spatial Planning Coordination Board, which was chaired by the Coordinating Minister for the Economy. The board's offices were set up in the National Development Planning Agency (BAPPENAS). The Directorate General of Spatial Planning of the Ministry of Public Works was charged with handling the practical implementation of the board's plan.

In October 2016, MOT issued a Letter of Import Approval (SPI) to BULOG to import 200 000 MT of corn. BULOG targeted delivery of the full allocation no later than December 25, 2016. BULOG conducted a tender to procure the imported corn, requiring that any bidding company must be a member of the Grain and Feed Trader Association (GAFTA), thereby excluding feed mills. BULOG intends to distribute the corn primarily to micro, small, and medium enterprises (SMEs) and to maintain national stocks.
Import tariff for designated grain, feed and oilseed products increased to 5 percent from the previous rate of zero enforced since January 2011.

COVID-19: Indonesia plans to relax restrictions on importing goods as one of its fiscal measures to combat the harmful economic effects of the COVID-19 coronavirus. The government is to also relax regulations related to the Food and Drug Monitoring Agency. The government is preparing several stimulus packages, including one that would expedite the import process for 500 importers with good reputations and another to reduce logistics costs in ports across the country.

On 9 July, the Indonesia’s House of Representatives passed a new law aimed to (i) empower farmers by developing agriculture market organized/managed by group of farmers and cooperatives and (ii) protect farmers by maintaining profitable price of locally-produced agricultural commodities. Among the measures that the Government can use to ensure profitability of local agriculture there are: import duty policy, selection of port of entry for certain imported products and administrative and quality requirement for imports (import licenses, certificates of origin, quality standards etc) (USDA Gain report, 23 July 2013).

A Forestry Long Term Development Plan (RPJP) for 2006-2025 accommodates the main national forestry issues that are part of the existing National Forest Program identified since 2001 as well as issues that may develop in the future. The forestry RPJP 2006-2025 is a long term forestry sector planning document. It is an elaboration of the forestry management goals set out in Act No. 41 Year 1999, of the vision and mission for a future Indonesia, and of the development vision of a safe, just, and prosperous Indonesia, with a vision and direction for forestry sector development over the next 20 years.  The Forestry RPJP 2006-2025 is established with the purpose of providing a guide and reference for all forestry stakeholders to realize the goal of forestry development in accordance with the mutually agreed development vision and mission. The goal of this Forestry RPJP is to maintain consistency in the management of forestry development from one period to the next in accordance with forestry resources management principles, without being affected too much by political change or other non-technical influences.

Regulation on The Control of Claims on Processed Food Labelling and Advertisements

The Indonesian Regulation HK.03.1.23.11.11.09909 (2011) on The Control of Claims on Processed Food Labelling and Advertisements permits a limited number of listed nutrient function and disease risk reduction claims. The Regulation applies to any food product or beverage that has been processed. Generally, any nutrition or health claim may only be used on processed food or beverages if they do not exceed a certain level of fat and natrium per serving (13g total fat, 4g saturated fat, 60mg cholesterol and 480mg natrium). The Regulation sets out certain exceptions from this rule, detailed in its annexes, whereby products exceeding these limits may still contain certain nutrient or health claims ("low in [name of nutrient]" and "free from [name of nutrient]" claims; claims related to fibre, phytosterol and fitostanol; certain disease risk reduction claims).

According to media reports, on 16 April 2014, the Ministry of Trade of Indonesia issued a new decree to regulate imports and exports of rice. The decree stipulates that the National Logistics Agency (Bulog) can import rice for purposes of price stabilization and to deal with emergencies. Private companies registered as manufactures importer (IP) can import rice to be used as raw material in industries, only if that kind of rice is not produced domestically. Similarly, registered importers (IT) are allowed to import specific varieties of rice for health purposes upon approval from the Ministry of Trade and the Ministry of Agriculture. According to the new regulation, rice exports are allowed only when supply in the country exceeds domestic requirements and any exporter other than the Bulog, must obtain permission from the Ministry of Agriculture (Oryza, 09 April 2014).

According to a media report, the government announced amendments in the “Rice for Poor” programme (locally known as Raskin) in 2014 in order to remove irregularities. The Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) reported several other anomalies in the scheme, including invalid data of targeted households, fictitious distribution of subsidized rice, prices hikes despite subsidies and poor rice quality. The government is committed to monitor accuracy, timing, quantity and quality of rice distributed as well as revising the scheme to contain costs for the state (Oryza, 23 April 2014).

The Minister of Social Affairs distributed emergency aid worth more than INR 941 million (US$ 81 000) to population displaced by eruption of Mount Sinabung in Karo (North Sumatra province), including food aid totaling 3 million tonnes of rice, dried fish and vegetables and other material (Portal Nationl Indonesia, 19 September 2013).

Food–based dietary guidelines – Indonesia

In 2014, Indonesia revised the 'Balanced Nutrition Guidelines' intended for the general public, but the guide includes specific advice for groups through the life cycle. Indonesia uses two food guides: 1) A rounded pyramid-like shape (Tumpeng Gizi Seimbang) which is meant to represent the principles of balanced nutrition (diverse food, food safety, physical activity and weight monitoring), including five food groups and their recommended portions; and 2) A plate guide (Piring Makanku, Porsi Sekali Makan) which illustrates the recommended proportions of food groups to be consumed in each meal. The plate also shows the importance of hydration and hygiene before and after meals.
Biofuel subsidies increased in fiscal year 2012, from IDR 2 000 per liter to IDR 2500/3000 IDR per liter for biodiesel and to IDR 3000/3500 per liter for ethanol.

The strategy for five years will concentrate to implement the missions, including to improve risk-based food supervision systems for protect the community, to encourage the independence of businesses in providing guarantees, and to change to pro-active control by encouraging community empowerment and partnerships with stakeholders.

Implementation of an integrated cropping management approach that encourages farmers to use certified seed, apply balance fertilizing in their field, and intermittent irrigation, since 2006. Rice import ban, in place since 2007, is extended until the end of 2010.

At these levels, Indonesian wheat imports are expected to contract to 8.5 MMT in MY 2016/17.
Implementation of a two-year moratorium on issuing new permits for conversion of natural forest and peat land starting from  mid-2011.

The MY 2016/17 total allocation for raw sugar imports by refineries is expected to reach 3.2 MMT. The GOI authorized refineries a total allocation of 1.6 MMT of imported raw sugar for the first quarter of 2017. As of March 2017, refineries have imported approximately 324 000 MT of the allocation. MOT authorized sugar refineries and state owned trading companies to import an additional 400,000 MT of raw sugar in early January 2017 to be processed into white sugar.

The government has doubled the upper limit of palm oil export levies to dissuade companies from exporting the product amid a domestic shortage of palm oil-based cooking oil. The Finance Ministry issued on Friday a regulation that raises the progressive levy up to USD375 per ton of CPO when international prices are above USD1 500 per ton. • The package provides a range of fiscal and non-fiscal incentives in addition to a special stimulus for small and medium-sized (SMEs) businesses. SMEs are eligible for loans of up to 10 billion rupiah (US$655,000) if they have a good credit history and have the capacity to pay back the loan.  
• The fiscal incentives are primarily for the manufacturing sector and include a reduction in corporate and personal income tax (includes food industry)
• Non-fiscal incentives aim to ease import and export activities: simplification of import and export activities, Simplification of import process for raw materials (includes to producers of strategic food items such as sugar, flour, and salt), Assisting reputable traders, Accelerate the implementation of the National Logistic Ecosystem (all logistic platforms, such as warehousing, shipping, and forwarders can access and share information. In particular, the measures are designed to keep the real sector moving and maintain purchasing power in order to boost domestic economic performance. The measures will be granted for a period of six months (i.e. from April to September 2020) and include:

• Relaxation of income tax on import.

• Acceleration to VAT refunds.

Program to increase rice production by 2 million tonnes since 2007 by providing free seed to farmers. The government announced a land area of ​​350 thousand hectares will be prepared in order to achieve self-sufficiency in sugar by 2014 (Portal of the National Republic of Indonesia, July 19th, 2011).

New import regulation approved for horticultural products, effective from 15 June 2012: all importers of fresh horticultural products, as well processed products derived from horticultural products, need specifically allocated import permits. These permits will be allowed only if domestic production and supplies are deemed insufficient.

The most recent RPJMN specifies that the green economy is to be the foundation of Indonesia’s development programme. The emphasis is to be on “inclusive and sustainable growth, increasing value added of natural resources with the sustainable approach, increasing quality of the environment, disaster mitigation and tackling climate change”. Other strategies included in the plan are: To create and to increase green cities development as a part of climate and disaster security through : (a) spatial planning which orientates on environment sustainability; (b) improved institution and capacity of public officer to mitigate and reduce disaster risks; (c) providing public goods and infrastructure based on green construction principles; To develop the rural and remote areas, with special attention on border areas, disadvantaged regions, transmigration areas, and small islands; To eradicate illegal logging, illegal fishing and illegal mining; To improve governance in natural resources and to increase community participation in forest

To support development in Papua and West Papua provinces and better connect it to other areas, the Government established the National Strategic Way to Accelerate Development West Papua and assigned the Indonesian National Army (TNI) to carry out road and insfrastructure construction under the supervision of the  Ministry of Public Works (Portal National Republik Indonesia, 29 May 20013)

In an effort to support and enhance food security and tackle high global food prices, the Government mandated the Public Company (Perum) Bulog to manage procurement and distribution of soybean in addition to rice (Portal National Republik Indonesia 22 May 2013).

Food Security Agency implements a Community Diversification and Food Security Improvement Program. Programs and strategic activities will be implemented at 34 provinces and around 513 districts/cities, among others: (1) Accelerating diversity food consumption, (2) Increased supervision of safety and quality of fresh food, (3) Community food business development through farmers’ shop, (4) Strengthening community food distribution institutions, (5) Strengthening capacity of food reserve, (6) Strengthening community food self-reliance, and (7) Management of chronic food insecurity.

In an attempt to stabilize domestic beef prices, the Ministry of Trade (MOT) issued a decree to allow imports of beef cattle by authorized business operators other than registered importers, during the period of 18 July - 31 December 2013. Operators are requested to apply for import permits via Trade Service Unit (UPP), and beef cattle import allocation per each will be set by the MOT by considering the capacity of their facilities (USDA Gain report, 24 July 2013)
As of October 1, 2016, a total of 97 U.S. dairy plants have been listed by Indonesia’s Ministry of Agriculture as approved for export to Indonesia, an increase from 90 in October 2015.

For the CY 2010, the Government allocated an amount of Rp. 1.6 trillion ($ 175,000) for seed subsidies, and Rp. 11.3 trillion ($ 1.24 million) for fertilizer subsidies, lower than Rp. 17.5 trillion ($ 1.9 million) in CY 2009. As a consequence of the reduced fertilizer subsidy, the Government may increase the maximum retail price of fertilizer starting from April 2010. 

Budget allocation: Rp. 12.9 trillion

Rice procurement price increased by 28.5 percent, to IDR 6 500/kg (USD 707/tonne), ahead of harvesting. The 2012 rice procurements are expected to reach 3.5 million tonnes, up from 1.6 million in the previous year, in an attempt to expand the subsidised sales programme for the poor.

After reducing the variable export tax on crude palm oil to 9 percent in September, the government is now considering to remove it because prices are lower than the average price set by the formula of the related regulation (monthly tax level is set by a formula based on average prices in selected market). As a consequence of the zero export tax, exporters will have free rein to lure more buyers amid unprecedented high palm-oil output in Southeast Asia to prevent a build-up in stockpiles

The Ministry of Forestry re-launched the National Forest Monitoring System (NFMS) to provide information on deforestation, remote sensing data and field measurements for the sector  (Ministry of Forestry, 31 October 2012).

The Government launched the draft RPJMN 2020-2024 for public consultation on 28 June 2019. The government target GDP growth rate of 5.4-6 percent in next five years, in which modernizing the agricultural industry aims to increase the sector growth to 3.8 – 3.9 per year, higher than 3.7 percent in 2018. Economic development will be encouraged to grow higher, inclusive and competitive through. Economic development will be implemented through two approaches, namely: (1) management economic resources, and (2) value increases added economy. Both of these approaches become the basis for synergy and policy integration cross-sector which includes the food sector and agriculture, maritime and fisheries, industry, tourism, the creative economy and the digital economy.

The implementation of these two focuses will be supported with the improvement of data to become a reference monitoring and evaluating development achievements, and improving the quality of policies. Expansion of the domestic economy is expected able to create an additional more than 9 million employment.

According to the Social Affairs Minister, the government allocated about Rp 18.9 trillion (around US$1.4 billion) for the 2015 Raskin program. Currently, the Social Affairs Ministry looks after the budgetary allocations for the program and the state logistics agency Bulog takes care of the distribution through local administrators.

The Agriculture Development Strategy (2015-2045) is formulated as part of the constitutional mandate to achieve a dignified, independent, developed, fair, and prosperous Indonesia, no later than 2045 which coincides with the 100 years celebration of Indonesia.  This is a momentous occasion to put spirit, and mobilize national resources to achieve the greatest vision as mandated by the constitution.  The GSAD is a continuation of the Longterm National Development Plan 2005-2025 and the Master Plan of the Acceleration and Expansion of Indonesian Economic Development 2011-2025. COVID-19: Governor of DKI has decided to transition out of large scale social restrictions in Jakarta from 5 June to the end of June. This decision has allowed for some public places such as malls to reopen while adopting Covid-19 protocols. However, some areas are still considered as red zones for Covid-19 and large scale social restrictions are extended.

Pakistan and Indonesia have signed memorandum of understanding (MoU) on rice import. Indonesian government will import up to 1 million metric tons of white rice from Pakistan from 2016 to 2019, which is estimated around 400 million dollars. The G2G agreement will be implemented by BULOG (State Logistics Agency) from Indonesia and Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) from the Pakistani side.
The government has lowered the rice procurement target to 2.75 million tons in the beginning of this month from the initially set 3.2 million tons due to slow pace of procurement.

The National Strategy to Accelerate Stunting Prevention (StraNas Stunting) is launched in August 2017. The government is rightly focusing on strategic spending for evidence-based interventions to improve nutrition and food security, sanitation, health care, and care-giving for mothers and children. The strategy will be implemented locally by attacking stunting together with local governments, teachers, health workers and parents. The program will cover all of Indonesia’s 514 districts by 2021, and across all of Indonesia’s 75,000 villages in 20024. In September 2018, Indonesia has committed to allocate US$14.6 billion for implementation of the Strategy, that aims to benefit 48 million pregnant mothers and children under 2 years old in the next four years.

In the context of achieving the 2014 target of rice surplus (10 MMT), flood-resistant and drought-tolerant rice seeds will be distributed to support national food security programs (Ministry of Agriculture, 7 November 2012).

The Climate Change Roadmap is prepared to cover a time frame of 20 years (2010-2029). Priority programs of the Roadmap are outlined in four phases of five years in the relevant RPJM (see Figure 1). The programs of the Roadmap will be integrated into the RPJMN 2010-2014. Further on, it will be considered in the strategic plans of each ministry/agency. The Roadmap recognizes that regional approaches are needed. The policy response to climate change has been tailored to the characteristics of the main regions: Sumatra, Jamali (Jawa, Madura, Bali), Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Nusa Tenggara, Maluku, and Papua.

As of mid-June 2015, the Government of Indonesia has the authority to cap prices of staple foods and other basic goods during peak demand periods including the month of Ramadan. The measure is aimed at ensuring price stability through setting prices in response to periods of price volatility. Earlier this year, prices of rice (the main staple) reached a record high however, they have since fallen slightly.

Due to a likely reduction in this year's rice output, the government has decided to import rice in order to maintain adequate stocks and curb price hikes. Extending drought conditions have affected about 418,000 hectares of rice fields in Indonesia, according to the Agriculture Ministry. The drought has damaged about 148,749 hectares of cultivated rice area mostly in West Java, Central Java and South Sulawesi.

COVID-19: On 31 March 2020, Indonesian President signs the regulations needed for cities and provinces to enforce what the government described as “large-scale social restrictions” amid the COVID-19 pandemic. The government regulation on “Large-Scale Social Restrictions” and a presidential decree on “Public Health Emergency Status” are based on the 2018 Law on Health Quarantine, which allows cities and provinces to shut down non-essential services and limit religious and social activities.

The Ministry of Agriculture is providing training to farmers on post harvest and packaging process to improve food safety and quality for agro-products (especially fruits) and meet export standards (Berita Pertanian Online, 08 March 2013).
Import  tariff on rice of IDR 450 (USD 0.052) per kg is reintroduced, following the improvement of supply from  domestic sources.

On March 24, 2016, Ministry of Trade (MOT) issued regulation 20/2016 on corn imports. The regulation classified corn imports into three categories: feed, food, and industrial use. The volume of corn that can be imported for feed, food, and industrial use will be decided via an inter-ministerial meeting. The regulation assigns BULOG as the single importer of feed corn. In order to import feed corn, BULOG must get an import authorization from the Ministry of State Owned Companies and an import recommendation from the Ministry of Agriculture.

On October 18, 2012 the Indonesian House of the representatives (DPR) plenary session passed a new Food Law, effective from its legislated date. The new Law on Food, Protection and Empowerment of Farmers has been approved with the goal of reaching self-sufficiency in key food staples, by regulating imports and exports according to domestic consumption needs, and by establishing a new food authority to supervise food production, procurement and distribution (USDA Gain report, 20 November 2012).

Measures adopted in order to sustain the domestic sugar supply through imports, in case of domestic shortage. Sugar imports remain prohibited only one month prior to the milling season, during the milling season, and two months after the milling season. Registered sugar importers are required to support farmers through purchases of sugarcane production if the price falls below IDR 7 000/kg (USD 764/tonne) at the farmer level.
The Government will increase the allocation to the hybrid corn seed subsidy program to cover 1.5 to 2 million hectares compared to 750 000 hectares area in CY 2015.

The Government will restrict the export of rice for only 100.000 tonnes. Furthermore, the rice might be exported only during the period of April-June. The quota allowed to be exported (0.3% of the total product) was believed not to break off the stability of domestic’s food resilience.

To cope with falling onion prices, the Ministry of Agriculture, asked specifically to local government to provide backup budget to buy onions from the farmers (Ministry of Agriculture, 08 December 2011).

Under the processing machine revitalization scheme the Government of Indonesia is providing reimbursement to sugar factories to (i) purchase new machinery up to 22.5 percent, (ii) increase installed capacity of the existing sugar mills through land intensification, and (ii) develop new sugar cane plantation and mills (USDA Gain Report., 01 March 2013).

The Trade Ministry issued the ministerial regulation No. 11/2022 to retract the domestic market obligation (DMO) policy that required palm oil producers to set aside 30 percent of their output for domestic consumption.

In response to the floods in Jakarta and South Sulawesi the Ministry of Health is providing  food assistance to mothers and children under the program “Exclusive breast feeding and complementary food” (MP-ASI) (Ministry of Health, 15 January 2013).
Export taxes on oil palm lowered from 22.5 percent in April 2011 to 17.5 percent in May 2011, due to lower export benchmarking prices for May 2011 delivery.

A new regulation by the Ministry of Agriculture and the Ministry of Trade revises the import policy for horticultural products with key changes including the obligation for registered importers to import 80 percent of the total allocation within a six month period (Jan-Jun or Jul-Dec) and the application of a reference price system for chili and shallot imports (USDA Gain Report, 17 September 2013).

Minister of Industry regulation 10/2017 “Facility to Source Raw Material in Efforts to Develop Indonesian Sugar Industry,”  was issued in March 20, 2017, to encourage mills and refineries to use domestically produced raw material as much as possible. It requires the integration of refineries and mills with cane plantations. According to regulation 10/2017, sugar plantations can be owned by refineries, mills, or in partnership with farmers. The refineries or mills must source at least 20 percent of their raw materials from the integrated sugarcane plantations initially.
Import tariff suspended for rice imported by the State Logistics Agency (Bulog).

During the 2015-2019 KKP Strategic Plan the marine resource management supervision sector and fisheries play a strategic role in supporting three development pillars marine and fisheries especially in enforcement sovereignty of marine development and fisheries in eradication and overcoming IUU Fishing. The Plan set the specific objectives and programmes against the IUU fishing in Indonesia which focused in settlement of Maritime and Criminal Acts, improvement of by-laws and regulations, monitoring and surveillance fishing vessel, increasing investment in infrastructure, and enhancing performance IUU database and using the IUU Fishing countermeasures.

In this National Plan of Action for Food and Nutrition (2011- 2015), the policy of food and nutrition is developed based on 5(five) pillar approaches of food and nutrition development which covers the following: (1) community nutrition improvement; (2) food access; (3) food quality and safety; (4) clean and healthy life style (PHBS), and (5) Institualization of food and nutrition. The policy of food and nutrition is to improve community nutritional status especially mother and children, through food availability, accessibility, consumption, and food safety, clean and healthy life style including nutrition awareness, and followed by strengthening multi sectorals and inter programmes coordination mechanism and partnerships.

Bulog, the stateowned procurement agency, signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to import 1.5 million tonnes of rice annually from Vietnam, until 2017 if needed. Further MOUs will be pursued with Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Myanmar.

The Bank Indonesia and the Ministry of Agriculture have jointly launched a new insurance scheme for beef cattle in collaboration with a private insurer. The scheme provides coverage for risk of livestock death due to disease, accidents and loss and it will reinforce the bargaining position and eligibility of livestock farmers in terms of accessing credit and other finance facilities (Bank Indonesia, 23 October 2013).

COVID-19: Ministry of Agriculture (MoA) had signed a MOU with 17 key food supplier and distributor to ensure food supply for price stabilization at consumer level on 11 prioritized commodities (rice, maize, beef, chicken, egg, sugar, cooking oil, garlic, onion, cayenne, and chili), taking into account not only food supply but also transportation and distribution issues.

The trade ministry removed the price ceiling on packaged cooking oil that was previously limited to Rp 14,000 per liter. In addition, the government has also decided to remove the obligation to supply the domestic market (DMO) needs for crude palm oil and olein due the high disparity between export and domestic prices. The government revoked the policy because there was a high disparity between world and domestic CPO prices due to the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict. There are also indications of ‘mafia’ practices that hamper the distribution of cooking oil to the public. In a number of areas, packaged cooking oil was suddenly available after the government removed the retail price ceiling but the prices skyrocketed.

On August 28, Ministries of Agriculture (MOA) and Trade (MOT) released new regulations on import of meat and meat products specifying rules and requirements to obtain import permission and setting a new reference price system, which calls for meat imports when local retail prices rise above IDR 776 000 (US$ 67) per kg. In addition, the MOA will no longer issue volume allocations, and pre-shipment inspection is no longer required. However, the MOT will determine import volumes through Import Approvals (USDA Gain Report, 12 September 2013).

Re-activation of the Farmers Market, a Public-Private approach between Ministry of Agriculture, iPasar Indonesia and Futures Clearing Indonesia that aims to provide marketing facilities for farmers to market their agricultural products directly to consumers using electronic devices / internet ie Auction Market.

Imports restrictions on beef. Imports can only be done to meet the shortage of domestic supply alone. In 2010, import quotas of meat reaches 120 000 tons, is currently limited to a maximum 90000 tons or less 30 000 tons. The Government will continue to reduce the import quota was gradually (Ministry of Commerce, 15 August 2011).

Ministry of Agriculture announced the initiative to develop the economy of disadvantaged areas as agribusiness through assisting agriculture extension, education and training and institutional strengthening. The objective is to utilize 2 million hectares of land in developed regions to harvest rice, corn, soybeans and other local products.
The Indonesian Biosafety Committee for Transgenic Products, established in July 2010, approves two transgenic maize varieties for food safety (namely MON 89034 and NK603).

Bulog has agreed to buy 50 000 tonnes of rice from Vietnam and is expected to import more rice to maintain stocks at a government mandated 2 million tonnes. In line with the deteriorating production outlook, and despite the self-sufficiency policy adopted by the government, rice imports are expected to increase significantly in 2014 and reach 1.2 million tonnes (both private and public), up from an estimated 500 000 tonnes in 2013.

In reaction to high soybean prices, the Ministry of Trade decided (i) to release 150 000 tonnes of on-the-water soybeans without a surveyor report (ii) to increase the soybean importation allocation of the State Logistics Agency BULOG to 60 000 tonnes until the end of 2013 and (ii) to set the November-December 2013 soybean import quota at 584 000 tonnes to be distributed to 19 registered importers subject to the new import regulation implemented since 12 August 2013 (USDA Gain Report, 30 August 2013).

According to local media reports, the Indonesian government has set aside IDR 2 trillion (US$ 173 million) to prepare for the potential impacts of El Niño on the country food security. Half of the budget is allotted to boost rice strategic stockpile with Bulog (state-owned logistics) from 400 000 tonnes to 1.7 million tonnes and ensure supplies in case of emergency (Vietnam Plus News, 8 May 2014).

On February 24, 2017, the Government issued Presidential Decree No. 20/2017, moving BULOG’s authority on issues related to the procurement, import, management of government stocks, and government purchasing prices of paddy and rice to the Ministry of Agriculture (MOA). BULOG will continue its role as the implementer of these programs, but all decisions will be taken by MOA. The regulation will expedite Indonesia’s ability to implement rice programs by removing the requirement that BULOG activities pass via an interministerial coordination meeting. However, this will likely result in limited MY 2016/17 rice imports, as MOA is expected to aggressively pursue rice self-sufficiency policies. MOA’s new authority will be valid for six months following the implementation date in February, covering the critical domestic procurement period during the first and second harvests.

According to some media reports, the Ministry of Agriculture had announced the additional import of 500 000 tonnes of rice to increase stocks in an attempt to mitigate possible negative effects of El Nino weather pattern. Subsequently, the government stepped off, announcing that BULOG, the government-owned food supply company, has enough stocks (1.93 million tonnes) to ensure food supplies in the coming months, therefore increasing imports will not be required (Oryza, 10 June 2014).

The 10 percent VAT on wheat and wheat flour (that was removed on February 2008) was reinstated.
The 5 percent import duty on wheat flour, removed on February 2008,  was re-imposed on January 28, 2009.
The import duty for wheat is zero.

According to media sources, the Government has further detailed its plan to revise the “Rice for Poor” programme (locally known as Raskin) in 2014 to make it more transparent and sustainable. The government will issue a Social Protection Card (KPS) to eligible households to get rice at a subsidized price of IDR 1 600 (US$ 0.14) per kilo. The government will update its database of households’ income information regularly, through village council meetings. New households whose earnings are below 25 percent of average national income will receive the KPS, while those that exceed that limit will be excluded (Oryza, 04 June 2014).

BULOG has set its procurement target at 3.2 MMT of milled rice equivalent for MY 2015/16. As of December 2015, BULOG realized approximately 2.0 MMT of the MY 2014/15 procurement target, with ending stocks at 1.439 MMT. BULOG normally meets 60 percent of its procurement target during the first main harvest period. Despite the delay in the MY 2015/16 first harvest, BULOG procurements totaled 1.8 MMT as of the end of June, 2016.

The program, Kawasan Rumah Pangan Lestari (KRPL), was designed to help rural women become self-sufficient in food production by promoting home gardens and has helped to reduce their individual household monthly food spending by IDR 195,000 (US$21.45) (Jakarta Post, 08 March 2012).

In late January 2016, the Government designated the Indonesian National Logistics Agency (BULOG) as the sole authorized importer for corn. BULOG assumed ownership of the detained corn shipments and then transferred the title to feed millers with an agreement that 20 percent of the imported corn would be distributed, at a set price, to smaller poultry farms self-mixing feed rations. Additionally, the Government decided that Indonesia will import 2.4 MMT of corn in CY 2016 at a rate of 600 000 MT per quarter.
Bulog agency has so far bought 2.2 million tons of rice from farmers and it has 1.7 million tons in its stockpile.
In 2010 three new wheat millers will begin operations with an estimated annual capacity of 1.5 MMT. Most of the new wheat millers will be located outside of Java.

The State Logistic Agency (Bulog) signed a memorandum of understanding  (MoU) with Myanmar to purchase around 200 000 tonnes of rice per year. Indonesia already has already MoUs in place with both Thailand and Vietnam.

According to media sources, the Indonesia's new President aims at achieving self-sufficiency in basic food items such as rice, corn and sugar with the next four years. Though the outgoing President had introduced self-sufficiency targets for several food items in 2009 following food price hikes, most of them have been left unfulfilled due to corruption and other scandals at various levels of value chain.

Implementation of an integrated cropping management approach that encourages farmers to use certified seed, apply balance fertilizing in their field, and intermittent irrigation, since 2006. Using the “Color Leaf Chart”, farmers are encouraged to match the color of leaves with the color on the chart to determine the best time for fertilizing the plant.

Import regulations for horticulture products were revised by removing explicit quantitative limitation for specific commodities for the July-December 2013 period, while licensing, packaging and labeling requirements are maintained (USDA Gain Report, 16 May 2013).

Indonesia announced lower expected procurement for May-October 2017, attributing a slight decline to lower blending rates required by military vehicles. As a result, May-October 2017 procurement is expected to reach 1.3 billion liters, implying total 2017 consumption will be closer to 2.8 billion liters. 2018 consumption is projected to reach 3.1 billion liters.
Ministry of Agriculture issued regulation no. 3/2017 which allows BULOG to buy lower or higher quality paddy or rice above the government purchasing price between March 2 and August 27, 2017.

In order to maintain stable prices of corn at the farm gate level, Ministry of Trade issued regulation number 21/2016 “Pricing Benchmark for Corn at Farm Gate Level”. The regulation states that BULOG, other state-owned companies, cooperatives, and private buyers can buy corn from farmers at set prices.

Thailand's Commerce Ministry and the Thai Rice Exporters Association (TREA) have agreed to supply around 175,000 tons of 5% and 15% white rice to Indonesia under a government­to­government contract, according to Reuters.

Four new flour mills with a total installed capacity of 500 000 tonnes per year installed and operational since 2008. Another new flour mill with a total installed capacity of 600 000 tonnes is expected to start its operation by mid 2009.

Type of implementation: public and private.

Under subsidized rice distribution programme - RASKIN 2010, the allotment of 13 kg of rice per family per month has been increased to 15 kg, by increasing the total amount of subsidies from the previous IDR 11.4 trillion (USD 1.2 billion) to IDR 13.4 trillion (USD 1.4) in the amended state budget.
The 5% duty appliead to soyabean oil import has been removed

Updated from the Indonesian Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (IBSAP) (2003-2020), the IBSAP (2015-2020) responds tonational priorities related to biodiversity management for achieving sustainable development goals. The current IBSAP comprises the principal guidelines to be taken into account by policy-makers in the biodiversity sector, and is also intended to serve as a key reference document for implementing programmes and activities in other development sectors, be they government, private, or civil-society sectors, at either national or sub-national level. The IBSAP also calls for the need to ensure consistency with actions carried out to implement other international treaties to which Indonesia is a Party. Improvements in the current IBSAP over the earlier version relate to the inclusion of: updated data and information on the latest status of national biodiversity presented in Kekinian Keanekaragamanan Hayati Indonesia (Current Indonesian Biological Diversity) published by the Indonesian Institute of Sciences (LIPI) in 2014; programmes and action plans to achieve the (22) national targets and the Aichi Biodiversity Targets; results of a study conducted on the economic value and utilization of biodiversity, sources of funding, and a strategy for mainstreaming biodiversity into the development plan; and identified capacity support needs for implementation (e.g. from institutions, data and information exchange mechanisms, monitoring and evaluation mechanisms). Four specific action plans have been formulated on the following themes: biodiversity research, data management and documentation; biodiversity utilization; maintenance and preservation of biodiversity; and capacity-building of biodiversity management.

The government of Indonesia has issued a new regulation on basic commodities prices, which allows the government to anticipate price hikes of certain commodities such as rice, whose prices peak during the festive seasons, according to local sources.

The Ministry of Agriculture will conduct a pilot phase on agricultural insurance during the growing season October 2012 - March 2013. This pilot aims to provide protection from crop failure, by providing financial compensation for working capital for next harvest. The scale insurance pilot project targets planting 3,000 ha rice with locations in West Java, East Java and South Sumatra. This test involves the participation of state-owned Agriculture to facilitate financing insurance premiums by 80% to farmers, where the remaining 20% will be shouldered by them. The premiums are IDR 180,000 per hectare (USD 144) (Ministry of Agriculture, 17 October 2012).

Indonesia’s Ministry of Trade (MOT) issued regulation 63/2016 “Farmer Level Purchase and Consumer Level Selling Reference Prices” on September 15, 2016. Reference prices are set to ensure availability and price stability for agricultural products for both producers and consumers, as per Presidential decree 71/2015 on essential commodities. The regulation covers seven commodities: rice, corn, soybeans, sugar, shallots, chilies, and beef.

COVID-19: Efforts by the central bank and government to keep consumer prices under control also reined in inflation. (Food) Inflation in Indonesia rose to 2.98 percent in February from 2.68 percent in January, driven by higher prices of garlic and cayenne, among other commodities. It could be due to the coronavirus as well as disruption of garlic supply and availability from the exporting country of China, but what is clear is that the price increase is due to a lack of supply.

In CY 2009, the government will subsidize 5.5 TMT of inorganic and organic fertilizers for an estimated subsidy value of  Rp. 17.5 trillion. The maximum retail price of the fertilizer the Indonesian government allows has not changed since January 2007. The maximum retail price for fertilizer ranges from Rp. 1,200/kg (US$ 101/ton) to Rp. 1,750/kg (US$ 147/ton).
In CY 2008, the government provides subsidized hybrid corn seed for a total of 350,000 ha of planted area. In CY 2009 the total area grown with subsidized hybrid corn seed raised to 400,000 ha.

he objective of the National Action Plan (RAN-MAPI) to address climate change is for it to be used as guidance for various institutions in carrying out a coordinated and integrated effort to tackle climate change. It states that addressing the impact of climate change should not be conducted by a few sectors alone, but that coordination between sectors and government ministries is essential to mitigation and adaptation efforts. The plan outlines the vulnerability of Indonesia to climate change and sets out immediate, short-term, medium-term, and long-term action to combat it.

The current national spatial plan, which was established as National Spatial Plan (Law No. 26/2008), covers 20-year period and it is to be reviewed every five years. The organization responsible for drafting the plan was the National Spatial Planning Coordination Board, which was chaired by the Coordinating Minister for the Economy. The board's offices were set up in the National Development Planning Agency (BAPPENAS). The Directorate General of Spatial Planning of the Ministry of Public Works was charged with handling the practical implementation of the board's plan.

The National Energy policy is set to provide the direction of national energy management to achieve energy independence and national energy security to support national sustainable development. In particular, it focuses on re-establishing Indonesia’s energy independence by re-directing energy resources from export to the domestic market, and aims to rebalance the energy mix towards indigenous energy supplies. This includes minimising oil consumption and nuclear energy, whilst increasing the exploitation and consumption of renewables and coal, and optimising gas production and consumption. Targets include a share of renewable energy in the energy mix of not less than 23 percent in 2025 and at least 31 percent in 2050 provided that its economical fulfilled; and an electrification rate of around 100 percent by 2020.

For products under the HST category, the reduction of duties (0-20 percent) will commence in 2012 to become fully implemented in 2018.

The Front of Pack Traffic Light Label 

In March 2015, the Iranian government introduced a new version of the Food and Beverages labelling regulation that introduced a front of pack traffic light label. It displays individual information on the fat, sugar, salt, trans fatty acids and energy content of the product to improve consumer understanding. Green indicates low or a little amount of the corresponding nutritional risk factor, yellow indicates a moderate amount and red shows a high amount, with thresholds set for each colour. For example, the thresholds for salt quantity are green - less than 0.3g of salt per 100g of food, yellow - between 0.3g and 1.5g of salt per 100g of food, and red - more than 1g of salt per 100g of food. The label is mandatory for all industrial foods which are manufactured in, or imported into, Iran. The label is not mandatory for traditional foods and outlet foods. This advanced labelling protocol was implemented step by step over a period of 18 months, extended for another 12 months, and is now fully implemented.

It promulgates visions and sets quantitative and qualitative objectives in developing the country’s economy and society over the life of the plan. 

The development plan translates the strategic vision through the following general objectives:
• Increase in the gross domestic product (GDP) at a rate of 9.38% per year during the plan period. 
• Generate 3 to 4.5 million new jobs based on the proportion between capital concentration and work that will be used in activities and projects adopted by the Plan.
• Diversify the Iraqi economy through achievement of  gradual increases in the rate of participation by other sectors in GDP, particularly the production, agriculture, and industrial sectors, along with tourism, which is a sector with some accomplishments and promise. It is also one of the sectors in which private sector activity plays a historically strong role. This role can be strengthened in the future both through generation of GDP and through the jobs it can generate.
• Strengthen the role of the domestic and foreign private sectors, either in terms of the magnitude of investment anticipated within the country, estimated at about 46 percent, or in terms of job opportunities. The plan seeks to expand and diversify the activities that the private sector invests in, particularly comprehensive animal and vegetable production projects; fisheries; tourism of all kinds; conversion industries, particularly those in which Iraq has a comparative advantage; passenger transportation merchandise, communications, as well as port and airport management; and education, health, and housing. This Poverty Reduction Strategy is a 5-years nationwide sectoral document in line with the goals of the National Development Plan (NDP) for 2018-2022. Main goal is reducing poverty by at least 25 percent, by 2022. The strategic plan envisages (i) improving standards of living; (ii) protection against risks and hazards; (iii) achievement of economic empowerment needed to turn the poor into productive individuals economically and socially integrated. These objectives will be achieved through (1) sustainable income from work; (2) improved health status; (3) improved education; (4) suitable housing and environment responsive to challenges; (5) effective social protection; and (6) emergency response activities. The Strategy gives particular attention to the issue of financing and the costs of each activity. Regarding domestic financing, resources will come from (i) annual allocations of the general investment and current budgets; and (ii) savings generated from decentralization, with a consequent increased efficiency of implementation and local community’s ownership of the activities. The Strategy focuses on specific priority activities for specific poor areas, among others (i) financial and economic policies; (ii) investment policy; (iii) monetary policy; (iv) agricultural policy; and (v) trade policy.To help eliminate hunger and malnutrition, the Strategy proposes school feeding programs in poor areas.In order of making agriculture more productive and sustainable, interventions will aim at (i) establishing local associations for small farmers to provide agricultural services such as water use, maintenance, mechanization, storage, cooling and transport in small farming communities; (ii) encouraging farmers to plant trees and create different orchards according to their suitability for the regions; (iii) stimulating the increase of agricultural production; and (iv) diversifying rural economic activity to include complementary or nutritious activities for agricultural production and generate new value added.Rural poverty will be reduced by improving living conditions in the areas through (i) connection of rural and poor areas to the public water network to grant water supply; (ii) meeting the need of poor areas for schools and reduce the existing gap, also taking into account the specificity of girls' education and giving priority to the training of teachers in rural areas; (iii) providing job opportunities for poor rural women; and (iv) encouraging graduates of agricultural and veterinary to establish agricultural projects and companies that provide employment opportunities in rural areas.To enable more inclusive and efficient agricultural and food systems, the Strategy envisages (i) the establishment of agricultural cooperatives to provide agricultural services such as marketing and finance; and (ii) creation of suitable jobs for women, enhancing and involving them in the agricultural sector, even with dedicated programs.The resilience of livelihoods to disasters will be increased training poor farmers on methods of agriculture and irrigation responsive to climate change.

These programmes are designed to take account of their geographical and economic handicaps, such as remoteness, insularity, small size, difficult topography and climate, and economic dependence on a few products. Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) regulates animal health and welfare. This is based upon Article 13 of the Treaty of the Functioning of the European Union which recognises animals as sentient beings and requires full regard to be given to the welfare requirements of animals. Council Directive 2002/99/EC is the main legislation with regards to animal health and welfare. Countries within the EU may choose to implement stricter regulations, providing that they are compatible with those set out in the Treaty. The regulations cover the protection of animals during transport, at the time of slaughter and killing, protection of animals for scientific and experimental purposes, and the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. The principle which EU law with regards to animal welfare is based upon include freedom from discomfort, hunger, thirst, fear, distress, pain, injury, disease, and the freedom to express natural behaviour. 
This Animal Health Strategy has 4 main objectives of ensuring a high level of public health and food safety, supporting farming and the rural economy, improving economic growth/cohesion/competitiveness, and to promote farming practices and animal welfare which prevent animal health related threats and minimise environmental impacts.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural policy, the European Union has been providing food to the Most Deprived Persons of the community. This “Food Distribution programme for the Most Deprived Persons of the Community” has been in place since December 1987. It was originally implemented under Council Regulation (EEC) No 3730/87, with the latest amendment entering into force on 15 February 2012 under Regulation (EU) 121/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council. The food distribution scheme is funded by the EU budget with a ceiling of €500 million per budget year from 2009 onwards. In 1987, the budget started from slightly less than €100 million per year. This is a voluntary programme for the member states with 20 of them taking part in 2012. The scheme relies on the distribution of products from Union intervention stocks, supplemented, on a temporary basis, by purchases on the market. This scheme will continue to run until the completion of an annual plan for 2013. 
The target group for this scheme are the most deprived persons in the EU, which has been defined as physical persons, including families or groups of such persons, who are recorded or recognised on the basis of eligibility criteria adopted by the national competent authorities to be socially or financially dependent, or who are judged to be so on the basis of criteria used by the designated organisations and approved by those national competent authorities.

Under the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), since the 2003 reform, the EU provides direct support to its farmers in the form of payments granted directly to them under certain support schemes. These include: the single payment scheme (SPS), the single area payment scheme (SAPS), and support schemes for farmers producing rice, starch potatoes, protein crops, nuts, seeds, cotton, sugar, fruit and vegetables, sheepmeat and goatmeal and veal and beef. Direct support of the EU is currently based on Council Regulation (EC) No 73/2009. The objective of the EU direct support is to provide a safety net for farmers in the form of a basic income as well as contribute to providing basic public goods delivered through sustainable farming. The budgetary ceilings for these direct support measures change every year. The yearly budget allocated by the EU is of around €40 billion.

The SPS entered into force in 2005 and is implemented by 17 countries of the EU, with the other 10 implementing the SAPS. 
The SAPS was offered as an option for countries joining the EU in 2004 and 2007 and will remain in force until 2013. It is a transition measure towards implementing the SPS. For the SAPS, the level of payment is calculated by dividing the country’s annual financial envelope by its respective utilized agricultural area. Under the SPS, support is granted in the form of a single annual payment dependent on the entitlement of the farmers. The three main options for calculating the value of payment entitlements include a historical, regional, and hybrid model. The historical model is based on the payments received by a farmer during a reference period, resulting in different aid levels per hectare. The regional model takes all payments received in a region and divides them by the number of eligible hectares, resulting in a flat rate. The hybrid model is made up of a mixture of the 2 other models. 
Cross-compliance ties the direct support for farmers with standards of environmental care, public/animal/plant health and animal welfare, penalising farmers who infringe EU law by reducing the support they receive. Cross-compliance covers directives and regulations which formulate “statutory management requirements”, which apply to all farmers, even if they are not receiving direct support from the EU. In order to help farmers better understand and meet the EU rules set up by cross compliance, every member state has established a Farm Advisory System. 

In addition to this, the EU established a set of rules on good agricultural and environmental conditions which farmers must comply with in order to receive payments under the CAP. 

The CAP reform in 2003 decoupled direct support to farmers, so that payments were no longer linked to production of a specific product. Up to 10% of the budget allocated for each Member states, is made available to support specific sectors for the purposes of: 
1) Protecting or enhancing the environment
2) Improving the quality of agricultural products,
3) Improving the marketing of agricultural products,
4) Practicing enhanced animal welfare standards,
5) Specific agricultural activities entailing additional agro-environment benefits
6) Payments for disadvantages affecting farmers in specific sectors (dairy, beef, veal, sheep and goat and rice) in economically or environmentally sensitive areas as well as for economically vulnerable types of farming,
7) Top-ups to existing Single Payment Scheme payment entitlements in areas where land abandonment is a threat
8) Support for risk assurance in the form of contributions to crop, animal and plant insurance premia
9) Support by way of mutual funds for animal and plant diseases and environmental incidents.

From 2012 at the latest, all of these coupled payments will be decoupled and integrated into the SPS, except for the suckler cows, sheep and goat and cotton schemes which may remain linked to the production of those products.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has established laws and regulations to govern the use and development of bio-technology. A major concern for the EU with regards to bio-technology is genetically modified organisms (GMOs), which is mainly regulated by Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003. The main objectives for these regulations are to protect human and animal health by introducing a safety assessment of the highest possible standards at EU level before any genetically modified (GM) food and feed is placed on the market; to have in place harmonised procedures for risk assessment and authorisation of GM food and feed that are efficient, time-limited and transparent; to ensure clear labelling of GM food and feed in order to respond to consumers’ concern and enable them to make an informed choice and to avoid misleading consumers; to set labelling requirements for GM feed which provide farmers with accurate information on the composition and properties of feed, thereby enabling them to make an informed choice. In order for GM food or feed to be allowed onto the European Market, it must go through an authorisation procedure. The first step in the procedure is the submission of an application for an authorisation for the placing on the market, which is followed by the preparation and the delivery of an opinion by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). The public is then allowed to make comments on the opinion, after which the European Commission prepares and adopts a decision.
EU legislation allows for countries within the EU to provisionally restrict or prohibit the use and/or sale of the GM product on its territory. Austria, France, Greece, Hungary, Germany, and Luxembourg have applied this safeguard measure to certain GM products within their territory.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has been regulating plant health and variety. The main legislation with regards to plant health and variety is Council Directive 2000/29/EC (amending Council Directive 77/93/EEC).
The main objective of EU plant health legislation is to protect the safety of food derived from plants and to secure the health and quality status of crops in the EU. The legislation regulates the trade of plants and plant products within the EU as well as imports from the rest of the world in accordance with international plant health standards and obligations. This is partially done through providing protective measures against the spread of harmful organisms. The legislation contains a list of harmful organisms that threaten plant health in the EU. This includes the establishment of the European Union Notification System for Plant Health Interceptions (EUROPHYT), which is a rapid alert system dealing with interceptions for plant health reasons of plants and plant products imported into the EU or being traded within the EU itself. EUROPHYT also contributes to the implementation of preventative measures by ensuring that the data on risks to plant and plant products is up-to-date and accurate. 
The legislation with regards to plant health is known as the Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR). The Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR) looks towards contributing to sustainable production through plant health protection; ensuring competitiveness of the agriculture complex; contribute to the protection of public and private green, forests, and the landscape, and to ensure food security. 
The selling and use of plant protection products and their residue in food is also regulated.  Council Directive 91/414/EEC is concerned with the placing of plant protection products on the market. No plant protection product may be used within the EU unless it has been scientifically established that the products have no harmful effects on consumers, farmers, and local residents and passers-by; they do not cause unacceptable effects on the environment; and that they are sufficiently effective against pests. 
Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 currently governs the maximum residue levels (MRLs) of pesticides in food and feed in order to protect the health of consumers. These are controlled by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). If any infringements of the Regulation are found, these shall be countered by sanctions of the product.

EU nutrient claims – Ireland

Regulation 1924/2006 establishes EU-wide rules on the use of specified nutrient content and comparative claims (ie levels of fat for a low-fat claim). As of January 2010, only nutrition claims as listed in the Regulation’s annex are permitted. In theory, these nutrition claims may only be used on food defined as "healthy" by a nutrient profile. This nutrient profiling restriction was due to be implemented in 2010 but no model has yet been established. Therefore, permitted nutrition claims can be used as long as the conditions for use of the claim as set out in the annex are met. Once nutrient profiles are established, nutrition claims may only be used on food products deemed "healthy", though two notable exceptions will apply: nutrition claims referring to the reduction of fat, saturated fats, trans fats, sugars and salt/sodium will be allowed without reference to a profile for the specific nutrient, provided the claims comply with the conditions of the Regulation; and a nutrition claim may be used even if a single nutrient exceeds the nutrient profile as long as a statement in relation to this nutrient appears on the label in close proximity to, on the same side and with the same prominence, as the claim (the statement must read: 'High [name of nutrient] content').

EU fruit and vegetable scheme – Ireland

The EU School Fruit Scheme, launched in the 2009-2010 school year, merged with the EU School Milk Scheme on 1 August 2017 into one legal framework based on the Regulation on the new School Fruit, Vegetables and Milk Scheme (Regulation EU No 2016/791). The scheme is funded through the EU’s common agricultural policy and supports the distribution of fruit, vegetables and milk and milk products to schools across the EU as part of a wider programme of education about European agriculture and the benefits of healthy eating. It provides financing to Member States based on the number of school children and level of development of the country. The implementation of the programmes is at the discretion of national or regional governments, but to receive funding, they must distribute fruit, vegetables and milk products in schools and implement educational measures, such as farm and market visits, educational material distributed to teachers and interactive games on education and nutrition, and regularly monitor and evaluate implementation. The Red Warning Label

On 1 January 2020, Israel introduced mandatory red warning labels for products high in saturated fat, sugar or salt. Maximum levels of salt, sugar and saturated fats are defined by the Ministry of Health specifically to apply to be applied to these red labels. Depending on their composition, foods and drinks can carry one, two, or three warning labels carrying these messages: high levels of sugar, high levels of salt, and/or high levels of saturated fat. Food and drinks manufacturers have been granted two deadlines by which to reformulate their products: 1 January 2020 and 1 January 2021. In the first stage, the following thresholds were set: 500mg of sodium, 13.5g of total sugars, and 5g of total saturated fats per 100g of solid food. Beyond these limits, solid foods will require a red label. For drinks (‘liquid food') these maximum limits are 400mg of sodium, 5g of total sugars, and 3g for total saturated fat per 100 ml. Starting with January 2021, both these sets of limits will be reduced, as follows: 400mg of sodium, 10g of total sugars, and 4g of total saturated fat for solid food; and 300mg of sodium, 5g of total sugars, and 3g of total saturated fat acid for drinks.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has been regulating plant health and variety. The main legislation with regards to plant health and variety is Council Directive 2000/29/EC (amending Council Directive 77/93/EEC).
The main objective of EU plant health legislation is to protect the safety of food derived from plants and to secure the health and quality status of crops in the EU. The legislation regulates the trade of plants and plant products within the EU as well as imports from the rest of the world in accordance with international plant health standards and obligations. This is partially done through providing protective measures against the spread of harmful organisms. The legislation contains a list of harmful organisms that threaten plant health in the EU. This includes the establishment of the European Union Notification System for Plant Health Interceptions (EUROPHYT), which is a rapid alert system dealing with interceptions for plant health reasons of plants and plant products imported into the EU or being traded within the EU itself. EUROPHYT also contributes to the implementation of preventative measures by ensuring that the data on risks to plant and plant products is up-to-date and accurate. 
The legislation with regards to plant health is known as the Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR). The Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR) looks towards contributing to sustainable production through plant health protection; ensuring competitiveness of the agriculture complex; contribute to the protection of public and private green, forests, and the landscape, and to ensure food security. 
The selling and use of plant protection products and their residue in food is also regulated.  Council Directive 91/414/EEC is concerned with the placing of plant protection products on the market. No plant protection product may be used within the EU unless it has been scientifically established that the products have no harmful effects on consumers, farmers, and local residents and passers-by; they do not cause unacceptable effects on the environment; and that they are sufficiently effective against pests. 
Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 currently governs the maximum residue levels (MRLs) of pesticides in food and feed in order to protect the health of consumers. These are controlled by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). If any infringements of the Regulation are found, these shall be countered by sanctions of the product.

Under the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), since the 2003 reform, the EU provides direct support to its farmers in the form of payments granted directly to them under certain support schemes. These include: the single payment scheme (SPS), the single area payment scheme (SAPS), and support schemes for farmers producing rice, starch potatoes, protein crops, nuts, seeds, cotton, sugar, fruit and vegetables, sheepmeat and goatmeal and veal and beef. Direct support of the EU is currently based on Council Regulation (EC) No 73/2009. The objective of the EU direct support is to provide a safety net for farmers in the form of a basic income as well as contribute to providing basic public goods delivered through sustainable farming. The budgetary ceilings for these direct support measures change every year. The yearly budget allocated by the EU is of around €40 billion.

The SPS entered into force in 2005 and is implemented by 17 countries of the EU, with the other 10 implementing the SAPS. 
The SAPS was offered as an option for countries joining the EU in 2004 and 2007 and will remain in force until 2013. It is a transition measure towards implementing the SPS. For the SAPS, the level of payment is calculated by dividing the country’s annual financial envelope by its respective utilized agricultural area. Under the SPS, support is granted in the form of a single annual payment dependent on the entitlement of the farmers. The three main options for calculating the value of payment entitlements include a historical, regional, and hybrid model. The historical model is based on the payments received by a farmer during a reference period, resulting in different aid levels per hectare. The regional model takes all payments received in a region and divides them by the number of eligible hectares, resulting in a flat rate. The hybrid model is made up of a mixture of the 2 other models. 
Cross-compliance ties the direct support for farmers with standards of environmental care, public/animal/plant health and animal welfare, penalising farmers who infringe EU law by reducing the support they receive. Cross-compliance covers directives and regulations which formulate “statutory management requirements”, which apply to all farmers, even if they are not receiving direct support from the EU. In order to help farmers better understand and meet the EU rules set up by cross compliance, every member state has established a Farm Advisory System. 

In addition to this, the EU established a set of rules on good agricultural and environmental conditions which farmers must comply with in order to receive payments under the CAP. 

The CAP reform in 2003 decoupled direct support to farmers, so that payments were no longer linked to production of a specific product. Up to 10% of the budget allocated for each Member states, is made available to support specific sectors for the purposes of: 
1) Protecting or enhancing the environment
2) Improving the quality of agricultural products,
3) Improving the marketing of agricultural products,
4) Practicing enhanced animal welfare standards,
5) Specific agricultural activities entailing additional agro-environment benefits
6) Payments for disadvantages affecting farmers in specific sectors (dairy, beef, veal, sheep and goat and rice) in economically or environmentally sensitive areas as well as for economically vulnerable types of farming,
7) Top-ups to existing Single Payment Scheme payment entitlements in areas where land abandonment is a threat
8) Support for risk assurance in the form of contributions to crop, animal and plant insurance premia
9) Support by way of mutual funds for animal and plant diseases and environmental incidents.

From 2012 at the latest, all of these coupled payments will be decoupled and integrated into the SPS, except for the suckler cows, sheep and goat and cotton schemes which may remain linked to the production of those products.

EU health claims – Italy 

Regulation 1924/2006 (applicable as of July 2007) establishes EU-wide rules on the use of health claims (claims on nutrient function, disease risk reduction and children's health). Companies may only use health claims that are substantiated and authorised by the European Commission and Member States (various regulations authorising health claims to date). The European Food Safety Authority is responsible for verifying the scientific substantiation of claims; it has done so for claims currently in use and continues to do so for claims that are proposed and applied for by companies that want to use health claims in the EU. In theory, health claims may only be used on food defined as "healthy" by a nutrient profile. This nutrient profiling restriction was due to be implemented in 2010 but no model has yet been established. Therefore, permitted health claims can be used as long as the conditions for use of the claim as set out in the respective regulations are met. Once nutrient profiles are established, health claims may only be used on food products deemed "healthy".

EU nutrient claims – Italy 

Regulation 1924/2006 establishes EU-wide rules on the use of specified nutrient content and comparative claims (ie levels of fat for a low-fat claim). As of January 2010, only nutrition claims as listed in the Regulation’s annex are permitted. In theory, these nutrition claims may only be used on food defined as "healthy" by a nutrient profile. This nutrient profiling restriction was due to be implemented in 2010 but no model has yet been established. Therefore, permitted nutrition claims can be used as long as the conditions for use of the claim as set out in the annex are met. Once nutrient profiles are established, nutrition claims may only be used on food products deemed "healthy", though two notable exceptions will apply: nutrition claims referring to the reduction of fat, saturated fats, trans fats, sugars and salt/sodium will be allowed without reference to a profile for the specific nutrient, provided the claims comply with the conditions of the Regulation; and a nutrition claim may be used even if a single nutrient exceeds the nutrient profile as long as a statement in relation to this nutrient appears on the label in close proximity to, on the same side and with the same prominence, as the claim (the statement must read: 'High [name of nutrient] content').

Council Directive 2002/99/EC is the main legislation with regards to animal health and welfare. Countries within the EU may choose to implement stricter regulations, providing that they are compatible with those set out in the Treaty. The regulations cover the protection of animals during transport, at the time of slaughter and killing, protection of animals for scientific and experimental purposes, and the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. The principle which EU law with regards to animal welfare is based upon include freedom from discomfort, hunger, thirst, fear, distress, pain, injury, disease, and the freedom to express natural behaviour. 
This Animal Health Strategy has 4 main objectives of ensuring a high level of public health and food safety, supporting farming and the rural economy, improving economic growth/cohesion/competitiveness, and to promote farming practices and animal welfare which prevent animal health related threats and minimise environmental impacts.
