Under the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), since the 2003 reform, the EU provides direct support to its farmers in the form of payments granted directly to them under certain support schemes. These include: the single payment scheme (SPS), the single area payment scheme (SAPS), and support schemes for farmers producing rice, starch potatoes, protein crops, nuts, seeds, cotton, sugar, fruit and vegetables, sheepmeat and goatmeal and veal and beef. Direct support of the EU is currently based on Council Regulation (EC) No 73/2009. The objective of the EU direct support is to provide a safety net for farmers in the form of a basic income as well as contribute to providing basic public goods delivered through sustainable farming. The budgetary ceilings for these direct support measures change every year. The yearly budget allocated by the EU is of around €40 billion.

The SPS entered into force in 2005 and is implemented by 17 countries of the EU, with the other 10 implementing the SAPS. 
The SAPS was offered as an option for countries joining the EU in 2004 and 2007 and will remain in force until 2013. It is a transition measure towards implementing the SPS. For the SAPS, the level of payment is calculated by dividing the country’s annual financial envelope by its respective utilized agricultural area. Under the SPS, support is granted in the form of a single annual payment dependent on the entitlement of the farmers. The three main options for calculating the value of payment entitlements include a historical, regional, and hybrid model. The historical model is based on the payments received by a farmer during a reference period, resulting in different aid levels per hectare. The regional model takes all payments received in a region and divides them by the number of eligible hectares, resulting in a flat rate. The hybrid model is made up of a mixture of the 2 other models. 
Cross-compliance ties the direct support for farmers with standards of environmental care, public/animal/plant health and animal welfare, penalising farmers who infringe EU law by reducing the support they receive. Cross-compliance covers directives and regulations which formulate “statutory management requirements”, which apply to all farmers, even if they are not receiving direct support from the EU. In order to help farmers better understand and meet the EU rules set up by cross compliance, every member state has established a Farm Advisory System. 

In addition to this, the EU established a set of rules on good agricultural and environmental conditions which farmers must comply with in order to receive payments under the CAP. 

The CAP reform in 2003 decoupled direct support to farmers, so that payments were no longer linked to production of a specific product. Up to 10% of the budget allocated for each Member states, is made available to support specific sectors for the purposes of: 
1) Protecting or enhancing the environment
2) Improving the quality of agricultural products,
3) Improving the marketing of agricultural products,
4) Practicing enhanced animal welfare standards,
5) Specific agricultural activities entailing additional agro-environment benefits
6) Payments for disadvantages affecting farmers in specific sectors (dairy, beef, veal, sheep and goat and rice) in economically or environmentally sensitive areas as well as for economically vulnerable types of farming,
7) Top-ups to existing Single Payment Scheme payment entitlements in areas where land abandonment is a threat
8) Support for risk assurance in the form of contributions to crop, animal and plant insurance premia
9) Support by way of mutual funds for animal and plant diseases and environmental incidents.

From 2012 at the latest, all of these coupled payments will be decoupled and integrated into the SPS, except for the suckler cows, sheep and goat and cotton schemes which may remain linked to the production of those products.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has established laws and regulations to govern the use and development of bio-technology. A major concern for the EU with regards to bio-technology is genetically modified organisms (GMOs), which is mainly regulated by Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003. The main objectives for these regulations are to protect human and animal health by introducing a safety assessment of the highest possible standards at EU level before any genetically modified (GM) food and feed is placed on the market; to have in place harmonised procedures for risk assessment and authorisation of GM food and feed that are efficient, time-limited and transparent; to ensure clear labelling of GM food and feed in order to respond to consumers’ concern and enable them to make an informed choice and to avoid misleading consumers; to set labelling requirements for GM feed which provide farmers with accurate information on the composition and properties of feed, thereby enabling them to make an informed choice. In order for GM food or feed to be allowed onto the European Market, it must go through an authorisation procedure. The first step in the procedure is the submission of an application for an authorisation for the placing on the market, which is followed by the preparation and the delivery of an opinion by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). The public is then allowed to make comments on the opinion, after which the European Commission prepares and adopts a decision.
EU legislation allows for countries within the EU to provisionally restrict or prohibit the use and/or sale of the GM product on its territory. Austria, France, Greece, Hungary, Germany, and Luxembourg have applied this safeguard measure to certain GM products within their territory.

Food–based dietary guidelines – Poland

In 2010, Poland published the 'Principles of healthy eating' one for the general adult population and another set aimed at school-aged children and adolescents. Poland’s food guide is the ‘Pyramid of healthy nutrition’. The pyramid is divided into six levels representing six food groups. Cereals are found at the base; vegetables and tubers on the second level; fruits on the third level followed by milk and dairy products, meat, fish, eggs and beans. Oil is at the top of the pyramid. A beverage group (represented by water) and images of physical activity are placed outside of the pyramid. Poland has also developed a pyramid for children and adolescents, almost identical to the one for the general population. The only difference is that there is an explicit recommendation to avoid table salt.

EU nutrient claims – Poland

Regulation 1924/2006 establishes EU-wide rules on the use of specified nutrient content and comparative claims (ie levels of fat for a low-fat claim). As of January 2010, only nutrition claims as listed in the Regulation’s annex are permitted. In theory, these nutrition claims may only be used on food defined as "healthy" by a nutrient profile. This nutrient profiling restriction was due to be implemented in 2010 but no model has yet been established. Therefore, permitted nutrition claims can be used as long as the conditions for use of the claim as set out in the annex are met. Once nutrient profiles are established, nutrition claims may only be used on food products deemed "healthy", though two notable exceptions will apply: nutrition claims referring to the reduction of fat, saturated fats, trans fats, sugars and salt/sodium will be allowed without reference to a profile for the specific nutrient, provided the claims comply with the conditions of the Regulation; and a nutrition claim may be used even if a single nutrient exceeds the nutrient profile as long as a statement in relation to this nutrient appears on the label in close proximity to, on the same side and with the same prominence, as the claim (the statement must read: 'High [name of nutrient] content').

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy, the European Union encourages the production and of biomass for energy and the use of bioenergy. The central legislation encouraging this production and use is the Renewable Energy Directive 2009/28/EC. The main objectives of this policy is to increase the security of the energy supply and to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. 
The legislation sets targets that the countries within the European Union will reach a 20% share of renewable energy by 2020. Within those targets, a 10% share of renewable energy specifically in the transport sector by 2020 goal has been set, of which liquid biofuels is expected to make the main contribution. Only sustainable biofuels can receive public support and be counted against the 10% target. The biofuels are also required to emit 35% less greenhouse gases than the replaced fossil fuel. This minimum requirement is raised to 50% from 2017 and 60% from 2018 for new installations.

EU health claims – Poland

Regulation 1924/2006 (applicable as of July 2007) establishes EU-wide rules on the use of health claims (claims on nutrient function, disease risk reduction and children's health). Companies may only use health claims that are substantiated and authorised by the European Commission and Member States (various regulations authorising health claims to date). The European Food Safety Authority is responsible for verifying the scientific substantiation of claims; it has done so for claims currently in use and continues to do so for claims that are proposed and applied for by companies that want to use health claims in the EU. This nutrient profiling restriction was due to be implemented in 2010 but no model has yet been established. The EU Fruit and Vegetable Scheme – Poland

The EU School Fruit Scheme, launched in the 2009-2010 school year, merged with the EU School Milk Scheme on 1 August 2017 into one legal framework based on the Regulation on the new School Fruit, Vegetables and Milk Scheme (Regulation EU No 2016/791). The scheme is funded through the EU’s common agricultural policy and supports the distribution of fruit, vegetables and milk and milk products to schools across the EU as part of a wider programme of education about European agriculture and the benefits of healthy eating. It provides financing to Member States based on the number of school children and level of development of the country. The implementation of the programmes is at the discretion of national or regional governments, but to receive funding, they must distribute fruit, vegetables and milk products in schools and implement educational measures, such as farm and market visits, educational material distributed to teachers and interactive games on education and nutrition, and regularly monitor and evaluate implementation. Foods containing added sugars, salt, fat, sweeteners or artificial flavor enhances are exempt from the scheme: as an exception, limited quantities of added sugar, salt and fat are allowed if they are approved by the Member States' health/nutrition authorities. The Member States determine the frequency and duration of the distribution of the food.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) regulates animal health and welfare. This is based upon Article 13 of the Treaty of the Functioning of the European Union which recognises animals as sentient beings and requires full regard to be given to the welfare requirements of animals. Council Directive 2002/99/EC is the main legislation with regards to animal health and welfare. Countries within the EU may choose to implement stricter regulations, providing that they are compatible with those set out in the Treaty. The regulations cover the protection of animals during transport, at the time of slaughter and killing, protection of animals for scientific and experimental purposes, and the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. The principle which EU law with regards to animal welfare is based upon include freedom from discomfort, hunger, thirst, fear, distress, pain, injury, disease, and the freedom to express natural behaviour. 
This Animal Health Strategy has 4 main objectives of ensuring a high level of public health and food safety, supporting farming and the rural economy, improving economic growth/cohesion/competitiveness, and to promote farming practices and animal welfare which prevent animal health related threats and minimise environmental impacts.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural policy, the European Union has been providing food to the Most Deprived Persons of the community. The target group for this scheme are the most deprived persons in the EU, which has been defined as physical persons, including families or groups of such persons, who are recorded or recognised on the basis of eligibility criteria adopted by the national competent authorities to be socially or financially dependent, or who are judged to be so on the basis of criteria used by the designated organisations and approved by those national competent authorities.

EU nutrient claims – Portugal

EU Regulation 1924/2006 establishes EU-wide rules on the use of specified nutrient content and comparative claims (i.e. levels of fat for a low-fat claim). In theory, nutrition claims may only be used on food defined as "healthy" by a nutrient profile. This nutrient profiling restriction was due to be implemented in 2010 but no model has yet been established. Therefore, as of January 2010, only nutrition claims as listed in the EU Regulation’s Annex are permitted.

If nutrient profiles are established, nutrition claims may only be used on food products deemed "healthy" though two notable exceptions will apply: nutrition claims referring to the reduction of fat, saturated fats, trans fats, sugars and salt/sodium will be allowed without reference to a profile for the specific nutrient, provided the claims comply with the conditions of the Regulation; and a nutrition claim may be used even if a single nutrient exceeds the nutrient profile as long as a statement in relation to this nutrient appears on the label in close proximity to, on the same side and with the same prominence, as the claim (the statement must read: 'High [name of nutrient] content'). 

The agency responsible for the implementation of this regulation in Portugal is the Economic and Food Safety Authority.

The School Distribution Scheme

The EU School Fruit Scheme, launched in the 2009-2010 school year, merged with the EU School Milk Scheme on 1 August 2017 into one legal framework based on the Regulation on the new School Fruit, Vegetables and Milk Scheme (Regulation EU No 2016/791). The scheme is funded through the EU’s common agricultural policy and supports the distribution of fruit, vegetables and milk and milk products to schools across the EU as part of a wider programme of education about European agriculture and the benefits of healthy eating. It provides financing to Member States based on the number of school children and level of development of the country. The implementation of the programmes is at the discretion of national or regional governments, but to receive funding, they must distribute fruit, vegetables and milk products in schools and implement educational measures, such as farm and market visits, educational material distributed to teachers and interactive games on education and nutrition, and regularly monitor and evaluate implementation. Foods containing added sugars, salt, fat, sweeteners or artificial flavor enhances are exempt from the scheme: as an exception, limited quantities of added sugar, salt and fat are allowed if they are approved by the Member States' health/nutrition authorities. The Member States determine the frequency and duration of the distribution of the food.

In 2018, the Ministry of Health, Education and Agriculture developed the Ordinance No. 113, which established the School Distribution Scheme. The School Distribution Scheme consists of complementary national regulations which guide the application of the EU Fruit and Vegetable Scheme. The School Distribution Scheme coordinates the distribution of fruit, vegetables and semi-skimmed milk and dairy products to children between preschool age and the 1st cycle of basic education (primary schools). Municipalities receive grants  to offer these products to preschool and primary school–aged children.

The Guidelines on Menus and School Cafeterias and the Guidelines for School Buffets

The National Program for the Promotion of Healthy Eating (PNPAS) collaborates with the Ministry of Education to develop guidelines for food supply in schools, including the Guidelines on Menus and School Cafeterias (2018) and the Guidelines for School Buffets (2012). These guidelines are mandatory.

The Guidelines on Menus and School Cafeterias (2018) are a fundamental document that promotes healthy food offer in all public schools, from pre-school to secondary school. They introduce a new and improved approach to food in schools, including vegetarian meals and meals based on the Mediterranean diet. The guidelines define recommendations on energy and nutrients requirements for each age group (from 3 to 18 years old).

The Guidelines for School Buffets (2012) apply to school cafeterias and to vending machines which provide food between meals to students. The guidelines set forth a guide for a healthy food offer, defining the food groups that: (1) can be promoted, (2) must be limited and (3) cannot be provided. School buffets must respect a 3 to 1 proportion between the food products that can be promoted and the ones that must be limited, respectively.

Foods that cannot be provided include confectionery, snacks, fast-food, processed red meats and sugar-sweetened beverages.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the EU provides export refunds for poultry meat. Council Regulation (EC) No 1234/2007 sets out the rules for providing the export refunds. This is due to the high input of raw material prices in the EU, which may cause the prices for certain farm products in the EU to be higher than the world price level for the same product. Export refunds are provided to exporters who must export their farmed goods to third countries, to bridge the gap between the EU price level and the world price level, to help them to better compete on world markets. The amount of the export refund can vary depending on the destination of the export. The values for the refunds must be fixed at least once every three months; however these can stay the same for longer than three months. The specific values can be found in the Commission Implementing Regulation mentioned in the comments.

Under the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), since the 2003 reform, the EU provides direct support to its farmers in the form of payments granted directly to them under certain support schemes. These include: the single payment scheme (SPS), the single area payment scheme (SAPS), and support schemes for farmers producing rice, starch potatoes, protein crops, nuts, seeds, cotton, sugar, fruit and vegetables, sheepmeat and goatmeal and veal and beef. Direct support of the EU is currently based on Council Regulation (EC) No 73/2009. The objective of the EU direct support is to provide a safety net for farmers in the form of a basic income as well as contribute to providing basic public goods delivered through sustainable farming. The budgetary ceilings for these direct support measures change every year. The yearly budget allocated by the EU is of around €40 billion.

The SPS entered into force in 2005 and is implemented by 17 countries of the EU, with the other 10 implementing the SAPS. 
The SAPS was offered as an option for countries joining the EU in 2004 and 2007 and will remain in force until 2013. It is a transition measure towards implementing the SPS. For the SAPS, the level of payment is calculated by dividing the country’s annual financial envelope by its respective utilized agricultural area. Under the SPS, support is granted in the form of a single annual payment dependent on the entitlement of the farmers. The three main options for calculating the value of payment entitlements include a historical, regional, and hybrid model. The historical model is based on the payments received by a farmer during a reference period, resulting in different aid levels per hectare. The regional model takes all payments received in a region and divides them by the number of eligible hectares, resulting in a flat rate. The hybrid model is made up of a mixture of the 2 other models. 
Cross-compliance ties the direct support for farmers with standards of environmental care, public/animal/plant health and animal welfare, penalising farmers who infringe EU law by reducing the support they receive. Cross-compliance covers directives and regulations which formulate “statutory management requirements”, which apply to all farmers, even if they are not receiving direct support from the EU. In order to help farmers better understand and meet the EU rules set up by cross compliance, every member state has established a Farm Advisory System. 

In addition to this, the EU established a set of rules on good agricultural and environmental conditions which farmers must comply with in order to receive payments under the CAP. 

The CAP reform in 2003 decoupled direct support to farmers, so that payments were no longer linked to production of a specific product. Up to 10% of the budget allocated for each Member states, is made available to support specific sectors for the purposes of: 
1) Protecting or enhancing the environment
2) Improving the quality of agricultural products,
3) Improving the marketing of agricultural products,
4) Practicing enhanced animal welfare standards,
5) Specific agricultural activities entailing additional agro-environment benefits
6) Payments for disadvantages affecting farmers in specific sectors (dairy, beef, veal, sheep and goat and rice) in economically or environmentally sensitive areas as well as for economically vulnerable types of farming,
7) Top-ups to existing Single Payment Scheme payment entitlements in areas where land abandonment is a threat
8) Support for risk assurance in the form of contributions to crop, animal and plant insurance premia
9) Support by way of mutual funds for animal and plant diseases and environmental incidents.

From 2012 at the latest, all of these coupled payments will be decoupled and integrated into the SPS, except for the suckler cows, sheep and goat and cotton schemes which may remain linked to the production of those products.

The Temporary Framework recognizes that the entire EU economy is experiencing a serious disturbance. Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) regulates animal health and welfare. This is based upon Article 13 of the Treaty of the Functioning of the European Union which recognises animals as sentient beings and requires full regard to be given to the welfare requirements of animals. Council Directive 2002/99/EC is the main legislation with regards to animal health and welfare. Countries within the EU may choose to implement stricter regulations, providing that they are compatible with those set out in the Treaty. The regulations cover the protection of animals during transport, at the time of slaughter and killing, protection of animals for scientific and experimental purposes, and the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. The principle which EU law with regards to animal welfare is based upon include freedom from discomfort, hunger, thirst, fear, distress, pain, injury, disease, and the freedom to express natural behaviour. 
This Animal Health Strategy has 4 main objectives of ensuring a high level of public health and food safety, supporting farming and the rural economy, improving economic growth/cohesion/competitiveness, and to promote farming practices and animal welfare which prevent animal health related threats and minimise environmental impacts.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has been regulating plant health and variety. The main legislation with regards to plant health and variety is Council Directive 2000/29/EC (amending Council Directive 77/93/EEC).
The main objective of EU plant health legislation is to protect the safety of food derived from plants and to secure the health and quality status of crops in the EU. The legislation regulates the trade of plants and plant products within the EU as well as imports from the rest of the world in accordance with international plant health standards and obligations. This is partially done through providing protective measures against the spread of harmful organisms. The legislation contains a list of harmful organisms that threaten plant health in the EU. This includes the establishment of the European Union Notification System for Plant Health Interceptions (EUROPHYT), which is a rapid alert system dealing with interceptions for plant health reasons of plants and plant products imported into the EU or being traded within the EU itself. EUROPHYT also contributes to the implementation of preventative measures by ensuring that the data on risks to plant and plant products is up-to-date and accurate. 
The legislation with regards to plant health is known as the Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR). The Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR) looks towards contributing to sustainable production through plant health protection; ensuring competitiveness of the agriculture complex; contribute to the protection of public and private green, forests, and the landscape, and to ensure food security. 
The selling and use of plant protection products and their residue in food is also regulated.  Council Directive 91/414/EEC is concerned with the placing of plant protection products on the market. No plant protection product may be used within the EU unless it has been scientifically established that the products have no harmful effects on consumers, farmers, and local residents and passers-by; they do not cause unacceptable effects on the environment; and that they are sufficiently effective against pests. 
Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 currently governs the maximum residue levels (MRLs) of pesticides in food and feed in order to protect the health of consumers. These are controlled by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). If any infringements of the Regulation are found, these shall be countered by sanctions of the product.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy, the European Union encourages the production and of biomass for energy and the use of bioenergy. The central legislation encouraging this production and use is the Renewable Energy Directive 2009/28/EC. The main objectives of this policy is to increase the security of the energy supply and to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. 
The legislation sets targets that the countries within the European Union will reach a 20% share of renewable energy by 2020. Within those targets, a 10% share of renewable energy specifically in the transport sector by 2020 goal has been set, of which liquid biofuels is expected to make the main contribution. Only sustainable biofuels can receive public support and be counted against the 10% target. The biofuels are also required to emit 35% less greenhouse gases than the replaced fossil fuel. This minimum requirement is raised to 50% from 2017 and 60% from 2018 for new installations.

In 2003, Portugal published the 'Food wheel guide' aimed at the healthy Portuguese population. Guidelines for the Provision of Healthy Meals by Social Care Entities

The Guidelines for the Provision of Healthy Meals by Social Care Entities present a set of basic guidelines for the preparation of healthy menus by social care entities. These include aid associations and groups, foundations, charities and other organisations which provide daily meals to various groups of the population, namely the elderly, children and socioeconomically vulnerable citizens. Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy, the European Union has set up programmes to help the EUs outermost regions in the agricultural sector, known as POSEI programmes. The main legislation which sets out the rules with regards to the POSEI programmes is Council Regulation (EC) No 247/2006. These programmes are designed to take account of their geographical and economic handicaps, such as remoteness, insularity, small size, difficult topography and climate, and economic dependence on a few products. The programme functions by specific supply arrangements, aimed at mitigating the additional costs for the supply of essential products for human consumption, for processing and as agricultural inputs, and measures to support the local agricultural production. 
The outermost regions of the EU, as identified in Art 349 of the Treaty for the functioning of the European Union (TFEU) are Guadeloupe, French Guyana, Martinique, Réunion, Saint-Barthélemy and Saint-Martin, for France; the Azores and Madeira for Portugal; and the Canary Island for Spain. 
The annual maximum funding for the measures provided by the EU are € 84,7 million for the French overseas departments, € 77,3 million for Azores and Madeira, and € 127,3 million for the Canary Island.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) regulates the intellectual property rights with regards to plant varieties. Council Regulation (EC) No 2100/94 covers the intellectual property rights, known as the Community Plant Variety Right (CPVR,) granted to plant varieties. The CPVR is granted to the person who bred, or discovered and developed a new plant variety or his successor. However these varieties must be distinct, uniform, stable, and new. Any production or reproduction, conditioning for the purpose of propagation, offering for sale, selling or marketing, exporting from the community, exporting from the Community, importing from the Community, or stocking for any of the previously mentioned purposes, will therefore require the authorization of the holder of the CPVR for that variety. CPVRs will last up to the end of the 25th year after the initial granting of the rights, or in the case of varieties of vine and tree species, up to the end of the 30th year.

The Farm-to-Fork Strategy has been developed by the European Union to accelerate its transition to a sustainable food system. The Strategy sets ambitious targets:
a reduction by 50% of the use and risk of chemical pesticides and the use of more hazardous pesticides by 50% by 2030.
a reduction of nutrient losses by at least 50% while ensuring that there is no deterioration in soil fertility. This will reduce the use of fertilisers by at least 20% by 2030.
a reduction by 50% of the sales of antimicrobials for farmed animals and in aquaculture by 2030
and reaching 25% of agricultural land under organic farming by 2030
Finally, the strategy also includes the aim for all rural areas to have access to fast broadband by 2025, to enable digital innovation.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has established laws and regulations to govern the use and development of bio-technology. A major concern for the EU with regards to bio-technology is genetically modified organisms (GMOs), which is mainly regulated by Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003. The main objectives for these regulations are to protect human and animal health by introducing a safety assessment of the highest possible standards at EU level before any genetically modified (GM) food and feed is placed on the market; to have in place harmonised procedures for risk assessment and authorisation of GM food and feed that are efficient, time-limited and transparent; to ensure clear labelling of GM food and feed in order to respond to consumers’ concern and enable them to make an informed choice and to avoid misleading consumers; to set labelling requirements for GM feed which provide farmers with accurate information on the composition and properties of feed, thereby enabling them to make an informed choice. In order for GM food or feed to be allowed onto the European Market, it must go through an authorisation procedure. The first step in the procedure is the submission of an application for an authorisation for the placing on the market, which is followed by the preparation and the delivery of an opinion by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). The public is then allowed to make comments on the opinion, after which the European Commission prepares and adopts a decision.
EU legislation allows for countries within the EU to provisionally restrict or prohibit the use and/or sale of the GM product on its territory. Austria, France, Greece, Hungary, Germany, and Luxembourg have applied this safeguard measure to certain GM products within their territory.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural policy, the European Union has been providing food to the Most Deprived Persons of the community. This “Food Distribution programme for the Most Deprived Persons of the Community” has been in place since December 1987. It was originally implemented under Council Regulation (EEC) No 3730/87, with the latest amendment entering into force on 15 February 2012 under Regulation (EU) 121/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council. The food distribution scheme is funded by the EU budget with a ceiling of €500 million per budget year from 2009 onwards. In 1987, the budget started from slightly less than €100 million per year. This is a voluntary programme for the member states with 20 of them taking part in 2012. The scheme relies on the distribution of products from Union intervention stocks, supplemented, on a temporary basis, by purchases on the market. This scheme will continue to run until the completion of an annual plan for 2013. 
The target group for this scheme are the most deprived persons in the EU, which has been defined as physical persons, including families or groups of such persons, who are recorded or recognised on the basis of eligibility criteria adopted by the national competent authorities to be socially or financially dependent, or who are judged to be so on the basis of criteria used by the designated organisations and approved by those national competent authorities.

Ministerial Order on the sale of unhealthy food and drink products at health institutions

In effect since January 2017, the Portuguese government bans the sale of a variety of unhealthy food and drink products at Ministry of Health and National Health Service institutions (Order No. 7516-A/2016). Banned products include salted products, cakes and pastry, breads with sweet fillings, delicatessen items, sandwiches with sauces, biscuits and cookies with more than 20g of sugar and/or with more than 20g of fat, soft drinks, sweets, sweet desserts, quick meals such as hamburgers or pizzas, alcoholic beverages, chocolates in portions with more than 50g and "snacks" defined as maize strips, chips, sweet or salty popcorn. The institutions were given six months from the date of the Order to remove the products, including negotiating contracts with vending machine companies. This law was later (December 2017) extended to cafeterias and buffets of the Ministry of Health and National Health Service institutions, by the publication of Order No. 11391/2017.

In 2015, Qatar published the 'Qatar Dietary Guidelines' intended for 2 to 65 year olds. The Qatar food guide is a shell-shaped plate that consists of six food groups: cereals and starchy vegetables; vegetables; milk, dairy products and alternatives; fruits; legumes; fish, poultry, meat, eggs and alternatives; the volume of which represents the contribution to a healthy diet. It is recommended to eat a variety of healthy choices from the six food groups on a daily basis. Foods high in sugar, salt and fat such as sugar-sweetened beverages and highly-processed products, are not depicted in the food guide.

Under the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), since the 2003 reform, the EU provides direct support to its farmers in the form of payments granted directly to them under certain support schemes. These include: the single payment scheme (SPS), the single area payment scheme (SAPS), and support schemes for farmers producing rice, starch potatoes, protein crops, nuts, seeds, cotton, sugar, fruit and vegetables, sheepmeat and goatmeal and veal and beef. Direct support of the EU is currently based on Council Regulation (EC) No 73/2009. The objective of the EU direct support is to provide a safety net for farmers in the form of a basic income as well as contribute to providing basic public goods delivered through sustainable farming. The budgetary ceilings for these direct support measures change every year. The yearly budget allocated by the EU is of around €40 billion.

The SPS entered into force in 2005 and is implemented by 17 countries of the EU, with the other 10 implementing the SAPS. 
The SAPS was offered as an option for countries joining the EU in 2004 and 2007 and will remain in force until 2013. It is a transition measure towards implementing the SPS. For the SAPS, the level of payment is calculated by dividing the country’s annual financial envelope by its respective utilized agricultural area. Under the SPS, support is granted in the form of a single annual payment dependent on the entitlement of the farmers. The three main options for calculating the value of payment entitlements include a historical, regional, and hybrid model. The historical model is based on the payments received by a farmer during a reference period, resulting in different aid levels per hectare. The regional model takes all payments received in a region and divides them by the number of eligible hectares, resulting in a flat rate. The hybrid model is made up of a mixture of the 2 other models. 
Cross-compliance ties the direct support for farmers with standards of environmental care, public/animal/plant health and animal welfare, penalising farmers who infringe EU law by reducing the support they receive. Cross-compliance covers directives and regulations which formulate “statutory management requirements”, which apply to all farmers, even if they are not receiving direct support from the EU. In order to help farmers better understand and meet the EU rules set up by cross compliance, every member state has established a Farm Advisory System. 

In addition to this, the EU established a set of rules on good agricultural and environmental conditions which farmers must comply with in order to receive payments under the CAP. 

The CAP reform in 2003 decoupled direct support to farmers, so that payments were no longer linked to production of a specific product. Up to 10% of the budget allocated for each Member states, is made available to support specific sectors for the purposes of: 
1) Protecting or enhancing the environment
2) Improving the quality of agricultural products,
3) Improving the marketing of agricultural products,
4) Practicing enhanced animal welfare standards,
5) Specific agricultural activities entailing additional agro-environment benefits
6) Payments for disadvantages affecting farmers in specific sectors (dairy, beef, veal, sheep and goat and rice) in economically or environmentally sensitive areas as well as for economically vulnerable types of farming,
7) Top-ups to existing Single Payment Scheme payment entitlements in areas where land abandonment is a threat
8) Support for risk assurance in the form of contributions to crop, animal and plant insurance premia
9) Support by way of mutual funds for animal and plant diseases and environmental incidents.

From 2012 at the latest, all of these coupled payments will be decoupled and integrated into the SPS, except for the suckler cows, sheep and goat and cotton schemes which may remain linked to the production of those products.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has been regulating plant health and variety. The main legislation with regards to plant health and variety is Council Directive 2000/29/EC (amending Council Directive 77/93/EEC).
The main objective of EU plant health legislation is to protect the safety of food derived from plants and to secure the health and quality status of crops in the EU. The legislation regulates the trade of plants and plant products within the EU as well as imports from the rest of the world in accordance with international plant health standards and obligations. This is partially done through providing protective measures against the spread of harmful organisms. The legislation contains a list of harmful organisms that threaten plant health in the EU. This includes the establishment of the European Union Notification System for Plant Health Interceptions (EUROPHYT), which is a rapid alert system dealing with interceptions for plant health reasons of plants and plant products imported into the EU or being traded within the EU itself. EUROPHYT also contributes to the implementation of preventative measures by ensuring that the data on risks to plant and plant products is up-to-date and accurate. 
The legislation with regards to plant health is known as the Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR). The Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR) looks towards contributing to sustainable production through plant health protection; ensuring competitiveness of the agriculture complex; contribute to the protection of public and private green, forests, and the landscape, and to ensure food security. 
The selling and use of plant protection products and their residue in food is also regulated.  Council Directive 91/414/EEC is concerned with the placing of plant protection products on the market. No plant protection product may be used within the EU unless it has been scientifically established that the products have no harmful effects on consumers, farmers, and local residents and passers-by; they do not cause unacceptable effects on the environment; and that they are sufficiently effective against pests. 
Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 currently governs the maximum residue levels (MRLs) of pesticides in food and feed in order to protect the health of consumers. These are controlled by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). If any infringements of the Regulation are found, these shall be countered by sanctions of the product.

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) regulates the intellectual property rights with regards to plant varieties. Council Regulation (EC) No 2100/94 covers the intellectual property rights, known as the Community Plant Variety Right (CPVR,) granted to plant varieties. The CPVR is granted to the person who bred, or discovered and developed a new plant variety or his successor. However these varieties must be distinct, uniform, stable, and new. Any production or reproduction, conditioning for the purpose of propagation, offering for sale, selling or marketing, exporting from the community, exporting from the Community, importing from the Community, or stocking for any of the previously mentioned purposes, will therefore require the authorization of the holder of the CPVR for that variety. CPVRs will last up to the end of the 25th year after the initial granting of the rights, or in the case of varieties of vine and tree species, up to the end of the 30th year.

The EU School Fruit Scheme, launched in the 2009-2010 school year, merged with the EU School Milk Scheme on 1 August 2017 into one legal framework based on the Regulation on the new School Fruit, Vegetables and Milk Scheme (Regulation EU No 2016/791). The scheme is funded through the EU’s common agricultural policy and supports the distribution of fruit, vegetables and milk and milk products to schools across the EU as part of a wider programme of education about European agriculture and the benefits of healthy eating. It provides financing to Member States based on the number of school children and level of development of the country. The implementation of the programmes is at the discretion of national or regional governments, but to receive funding, they must distribute fruit, vegetables and milk products in schools and implement educational measures, such as farm and market visits, educational material distributed to teachers and interactive games on education and nutrition, and regularly monitor and evaluate implementation. Foods containing added sugars, salt, fat, sweeteners or artificial flavor enhances are exempt from the scheme: as an exception, limited quantities of added sugar, salt and fat are allowed if they are approved by the Member States' health/nutrition authorities. The Member States determine the frequency and duration of the distribution of the food.

EU nutrient claims – Romania

Regulation 1924/2006 establishes EU-wide rules on the use of specified nutrient content and comparative claims (ie levels of fat for a low-fat claim). As of January 2010, only nutrition claims as listed in the Regulation’s annex are permitted. In theory, these nutrition claims may only be used on food defined as "healthy" by a nutrient profile. This nutrient profiling restriction was due to be implemented in 2010 but no model has yet been established. Therefore, permitted nutrition claims can be used as long as the conditions for use of the claim as set out in the annex are met. Once nutrient profiles are established, nutrition claims may only be used on food products deemed "healthy", though two notable exceptions will apply: nutrition claims referring to the reduction of fat, saturated fats, trans fats, sugars and salt/sodium will be allowed without reference to a profile for the specific nutrient, provided the claims comply with the conditions of the Regulation; and a nutrition claim may be used even if a single nutrient exceeds the nutrient profile as long as a statement in relation to this nutrient appears on the label in close proximity to, on the same side and with the same prominence, as the claim (the statement must read: 'High [name of nutrient] content').

Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy, the European Union encourages the production and of biomass for energy and the use of bioenergy. The central legislation encouraging this production and use is the Renewable Energy Directive 2009/28/EC. The main objectives of this policy is to increase the security of the energy supply and to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. 
The legislation sets targets that the countries within the European Union will reach a 20% share of renewable energy by 2020. Within those targets, a 10% share of renewable energy specifically in the transport sector by 2020 goal has been set, of which liquid biofuels is expected to make the main contribution. Only sustainable biofuels can receive public support and be counted against the 10% target. The biofuels are also required to emit 35% less greenhouse gases than the replaced fossil fuel. Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has established laws and regulations to govern the use and development of bio-technology. A major concern for the EU with regards to bio-technology is genetically modified organisms (GMOs), which is mainly regulated by Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003. The main objectives for these regulations are to protect human and animal health by introducing a safety assessment of the highest possible standards at EU level before any genetically modified (GM) food and feed is placed on the market; to have in place harmonised procedures for risk assessment and authorisation of GM food and feed that are efficient, time-limited and transparent; to ensure clear labelling of GM food and feed in order to respond to consumers’ concern and enable them to make an informed choice and to avoid misleading consumers; to set labelling requirements for GM feed which provide farmers with accurate information on the composition and properties of feed, thereby enabling them to make an informed choice. In order for GM food or feed to be allowed onto the European Market, it must go through an authorisation procedure. The first step in the procedure is the submission of an application for an authorisation for the placing on the market, which is followed by the preparation and the delivery of an opinion by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). The public is then allowed to make comments on the opinion, after which the European Commission prepares and adopts a decision.
EU legislation allows for countries within the EU to provisionally restrict or prohibit the use and/or sale of the GM product on its territory. Austria, France, Greece, Hungary, Germany, and Luxembourg have applied this safeguard measure to certain GM products within their territory.

On September 17, the European Commission presented its 2030 Climate Target Plan, in which the main objective is the reduction of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to at least 55 percent below 1990 levels by 2030. Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) provides funding to promote EU farm products. Roughly 50million Euros is allocated annually in financial support for campaigns to promote farm products and inform consumers about how they were produced. Regulation 3/2008 sets out the rules with regards to the promotion of the farm products. The promotional activities supported by these campaigns can include advertising campaigns in the press, on television, radio, or on the internet; point-of-sale promotion; public relations campaigns; participations in exhibitions and fairs, and a range of other activities.
 The EU financing can cover up to half of the cost of the campaign, with the professional organisation contributing a minimum of 20%, and the national authorities providing the rest. EU contribution can rise up to 60% if the measures are for promotion of fruits and vegetables intended specifically for children in EU schools as well as for those concerning information on responsible drinking patterns and harm linked to hazardous alcohol consumption. These programmes should be multi-annual and extensive enough to have an impact on the target market.

The government approved the Long-term Strategy for the Development of the Grain Complex of the Russian Federation until 2035 (hereinafter - the Strategy).

The purpose of the Strategy is the formation of a highly efficient, scientifically and innovatively oriented, competitive and investment-attractive balanced system for the production, processing, storage and sale of the main grain and leguminous crops, their processed products, guaranteeing the country's food security, fully satisfying domestic needs and creating significant export potential.

The implementation of the Strategy will increase the efficiency and manufacturability of grain complex enterprises, strengthen Russia's position in the world grain and grain products market, and will have a comprehensive impact on related industries, including by supporting the demand for engineering products, fertilizer and plant protection products.

The government approved the Concept of the demographic policy of the Far East for the period until 2025 (hereinafter - the Concept).

The concept defines the goals, objectives, mechanisms and main directions of state policy in the field of demographic development of the constituent entities of the Federation included in the Far Eastern Federal District, and is aimed at stabilizing the population of the Far East by 2020 and creating conditions for its natural and migratory growth by 2025.

The concept provides:

- population growth up to 6.5 million people due to natural and migration growth, attracting to the regions of the Far East for permanent residence of residents of other regions, compatriots living abroad, qualified foreign specialists and young people;

- increase the value of the total birth rate to 2.05; reduction of mortality from all causes to the level of 11.5 cases per 1 thousand people;

- increase in life expectancy up to 74.2 years;

- creating conditions for a further increase in the population of the Far East to 7 million people.

The concept contains the values ​​of the main demographic indicators for 2017–2025 in the context of the constituent entities of the Federation included in the Far Eastern Federal District, which are determined on the basis of proposals from the executive authorities of these regions.

The concept is planned to be implemented in two stages.

At the first stage (2017–2020), a set of measures is envisaged aimed at improving the demographic situation and stabilizing the population of the Far East.

At the second stage (2021–2025), actions are planned to ensure a natural and migratory increase in the population of the Far East.

The unified plan for achieving the national development goals of the Russian Federation for the period up to 2024 was approved in order to implement the Decree of the President of the Russian Federation dated May 7, 2018 No. 204 “On national goals and strategic objectives for the development of the Russian Federation for the period until 2024”.

The national development goals of the Russian Federation are of “interprogramme” (“interproject”) nature: the achievement of any of the national goals cannot be ensured within the framework of only one state program and (or) a national project (program). In addition, national development goals are closely interlinked. Achieving some goals is directly dependent on the achievement of others. Thus, halving the poverty level is impossible without sustainable economic growth. Labor productivity growth is not possible without the widespread adoption of digital technology and innovative development.

The unified plan to achieve the national development goals of the Russian Federation for the period up to 2024 represents the trajectory of the indicators characterizing these goals reaching the target levels, as well as a list of tools and mechanisms aimed at their achievement, regardless of belonging to state programs and national projects ( programs).

The government approved the Export Development Strategy for the agricultural engineering industry until 2025 (hereinafter - the Strategy).

The strategy characterizes the state of the industry and determines the basic principles of state policy in the field of supporting the export of agricultural machinery for the medium term.

The draft Strategy was developed in accordance with Federal Law dated June 28, 2014 No. 172-ФЗ “On Strategic Planning in the Russian Federation”, taking into account the Forecast of the Long-Term Socio-Economic Development of the Russian Federation for the Period until 2030, and the Forecast of Scientific and Technological Development of the Russian Federation until 2030 year , government programs "development of industry and increase its competitiveness" , "development of foreign economic activity" , Strategies for development of agricultural engineering of Russia on the item IRS until 2030 (approved by the Decree of the Government on July 7, 2017 No. 1455-p).

The purpose of the Strategy is accelerated export growth in the agricultural engineering industry.

The strategy envisages providing support to Russian manufacturers of agricultural machinery, expanding the range of products, creating conditions for sustainable growth in exports of Russian agricultural machinery products.

Strategy Objectives:

- an increase in the volume of deliveries of products of Russian agricultural engineering in traditional markets;

- expansion of the geography of deliveries of products of Russian agricultural engineering;

- involvement of new domestic manufacturers in export deliveries.

As a result of the implementation of the Strategy, it is planned to increase the volume of export of agricultural machinery - from 10,255 million rubles in 2018 to 30,220 million rubles by 2025. The number of enterprises exporting domestic agricultural machinery products should increase from 48 in 2018 to 70 by 2025 (more than 80% of all domestic enterprises). The number of countries - importers of Russian agricultural engineering products should increase from 35 countries in 2018 to 65 by 2025. It is planned that each of the market segments individually will show a two-fold or more increase in exported products.

The implementation of the Strategy will allow for the formation of a structured approach to solving the key problems facing domestic manufacturers and exporters, and will contribute to an increase in the load of production capacities and production volumes of agricultural machinery, and an increase in demand for raw materials, components and materials of Russian production.

The government approved the Federal Scientific and Technical Program for the Development of Genetic Technologies for 2019–2027 (hereinafter - the Program).

The main goals of the Program are a comprehensive solution to the problems of the accelerated development of genetic technologies, including genetic editing technologies, the creation of scientific and technological reserves for medicine, agriculture and industry, the improvement of the biological emergency prevention and control system in this area.

Directions for the implementation of the Program: biosafety and ensuring technological independence, genetic technologies for the development of agriculture, medicine, industrial microbiology.

The program provides for the creation and development on the basis of scientific and educational organizations of laboratories and centers conducting research in the field of genetic technologies, their technical support, research and development using genetic technologies, including the development of biological drugs, diagnostic systems and immunobiological agents for healthcare, biotechnology for agriculture and industry.

It is expected that as a result of the implementation of the Program, scientific and technological reserves for medicine, agriculture and industry will be created. Using genetic editing technologies, plant and animal lines will be developed, including aquaculture, in demand in the real sector of the economy. It is also planned to develop models of human diseases using genetic technologies in vitro and in vivo, the functioning of bioresource centers that ensure the formation, storage and provision of collection samples in accordance with international standards, the creation of bioinformation and genetic databases, the creation of at least three world-class genomic research centers . The development of biological preparations, diagnostic systems and immunobiological agents for healthcare will be ensured,

The program provides for the formation of a plan for its implementation for each three-year period and a comprehensive research plan. The responsible executor and coordinator of the Program is the Ministry of Education and Science of Russia. Methodological, informational, analytical and organizational support for the implementation of the Program is assigned to the Kurchatov Institute, which is the main scientific organization of the Program.

Implementation of the Program will be financed within the framework of state programs “Scientific and Technological Development of the Russian Federation” (including within the framework of the national project “Science”), “Development of Education”, “Development of Health Care”, “Development of Industry and Increasing Its Competitiveness”, “Development pharmaceutical and medical industry ”for 2013–2020,“ Information Society (2011–2020), ”the State Program for the Development of Agriculture and Regulation of Agricultural Products, Raw Materials and food, as well as due to budgetary appropriations of the budgets of the constituent entities of the Federation and extrabudgetary sources.

The government approved the Strategy for the development of Russian seaports in the Caspian basin, rail and road approaches to them until 2030 (hereinafter - the Strategy).

The Strategy was developed taking into account the Concept of long-term socio-economic development of the Russian Federation for the period until 2020 (approved by the Government Decree of November 17, 2008 No. 1662-r), the Concept for the demographic policy of the Russian Federation for the period until 2025 (approved by Decree of the President of Russia of 9 October 2007 №1351), the national security Strategy of the Russian Federation (approved by the Decree of the President of Russia on December 31, 2015 №683), Program of action for the strategic interests of the Russian F eration in the Caspian region in the 2016-2018 years.

The main goal of the Strategy is to strengthen the economic and geopolitical presence of Russia in the Caspian Sea, expand and deepen economic and cultural ties with the countries of the Caspian basin, create conditions for additional socio-economic development of the Caspian region of Russia by increasing the flow of international trade passing through the ports of the Caspian basin.

Targeted directions for the implementation of the Strategy:

- development of the Russian Caspian transport hub and its inclusion in the international trade system;

- creating a sustainable transport and logistics corridor with Iran, India and the Gulf countries;

- socio-economic development of the Caspian region;

- development of export-oriented business in the Caspian region through the Russian Caspian transport hub;

- reduction of existing logistics costs;

- Strengthening the country's defense and security in the Caspian.

The strategy provides for the solution of regulatory, tariff, investment, operational and institutional tasks.

Regulatory tasks include improving the competitiveness of freight and passenger traffic through Russian Caspian ports by simplifying administrative procedures (including speeding up customs procedures during cargo transportation, prompt coordination of projects to modernize port infrastructure), creating favorable conditions for the development of domestic and international tourism in this region (including simplification of the customs regime).

Tariff tasks - the formation and administration of uniform competitive tariffs for transportation through the Caspian transport hub.

Investment objectives are the modernization of the existing and the creation of a new logistics and transport infrastructure for the development of freight and passenger transportation, including port infrastructure, as well as long and near road and rail approaches to seaports.

Operational objectives - the introduction of a planning and project management system that reveals the export potential of the Caspian region, in particular production and logistics clusters, by creating the necessary legislative and administrative conditions and institutions.

Institutional tasks are the creation of incentives for the development of agriculture and industrial production, which, together with the development of transport infrastructure, can provide a synergistic effect for the development of the region, including the formation of development institutions and support for such projects.

The strategy is planned to be implemented in three stages: the first stage (until 2020) - preparatory, the second stage (2020–2025) - the main, the third stage (2026–2030) - promising.

Target directions, tasks, mechanisms for implementing the Strategy are aimed at creating a sustainable transport and logistics corridor, developing trade and tourism, primarily with Iran, India and the Persian Gulf countries. As part of the promising stage of the Strategy implementation, it is planned to study the issue of developing trade relations with all the Caspian countries, taking into account the expansion of the capacities of the new deep-sea port (terminal).

The implementation of the Strategy and the fulfillment of its indicators will allow to ensure grain export volumes through the ports of the Caspian basin up to 7 million tons by 2030, and the volume of freight traffic on other dry cargoes up to 7 million tons; to attract the Russian tourist flow to the Caspian region - up to 30 thousand people a year; create more than 2 thousand new jobs.

The government approved the Strategy for the Development of the Forestry Complex of the Russian Federation until 2030 (hereinafter - the Strategy). This is an industry strategic planning document that defines goals and objectives, ways to achieve them, priorities, stages of implementation of state policy in the field of forestry development in Russia.

The strategy is aimed at increasing the long-term competitiveness of the forest industry, increasing the contribution of the forest sector to the country's socio-economic development, the efficient use, protection, reproduction of forests by achieving sustainable forest management.

The main directions of the Strategy are the development of export-oriented production of pulp, the growth of the production of container board and sanitary products for the domestic market, the development of the production of lumber, plywood-plate production, furniture, and wooden housing construction, oriented equally to the domestic market.

By 2030, it is planned to significantly increase the contribution of the forest sector to the country's economy. An increase in the added value created by industry enterprises is expected in the amount of up to 676 billion rubles; increase in the contribution of the forest complex to gross domestic product from 0.5% to 1%; an increase in tax revenues to budgets of all levels from 91 to 189 billion rubles.

The implementation of the Strategy will allow the formation of an economically sustainable, globally competitive group of industries that provides domestic demand for forest products that is built into the world market and the international division of labor and operates on the basis of sustainable forest management and the preservation of the biosphere role of forests.

The government approved the Engineering Development Strategy for the food and processing industry until 2030 (hereinafter - the Strategy).

Providing food and processing industries with modern and high-tech domestic equipment is a necessary condition for increasing the competitiveness of products, maintaining the country's food security and developing export potential.

The goal of the Strategy is to triple the volume of sales of domestic products by 2030.

The strategy provides for an increase in the share of domestic machinery and equipment for the food and processing industry in the domestic market to 62%, an increase in export deliveries by at least 10% annually, an increase in the share of costs for research and development in the total revenue of enterprises of at least than up to 2%. The strategy is planned to be implemented in three stages.

The strategy is planned to be implemented within the framework of the state program “Development of industry and increasing its competitiveness” and the national project “International Cooperation and Export”.

The implementation of the Strategy will contribute to the opening of new production capacities, the creation of high-performance jobs, the technological independence of the food industry from imported engineering products, and the growth of export deliveries of Russian machines.

The main objective of the Programme, which updates and replaces measures of the previous State Policy on Energy Efficiency Increase through the Use of Renewables for the Period up to 2020 (2009), is to “ensure reliable supply of the country’s fuel and energy resources, increase the efficiency of their use, and reduce of anthropogenic impacts of the energy sector on the environment”.

This new version keeps the target of a 40% decrease of energy intensity of the economy between 2007 and 2020, but alters the 4.5% share of electricity generation from renewable energy sources target to 2.5% by 2020 (excluding large hydro over 25 MW). The Programme calls for diverse measures to attain those targets, including:
– evaluating the technological and economic potential of efficient renewables use
– providing subsidies from the state budget in order to compensate for the costs of grid connection for renewables
– installation of smart meters (18.9% of metering devices by 2020)
– increasing the availability of energy infrastructure – reducing the number of steps required to gain access to the grid (from 8 to 5) and reducing the delay of connection to the grid (from 276 to 40 days)
– raising public awareness on energy conservation and energy efficiency.

The State Programme is composed of seven sub-programmes:
– SP1: Energy conservation and energy efficiency improvement
– SP2: Development and modernisation of the power industry
– SP3: Development of the oil industry
– SP4: Development of the gas industry
– SP5: Restructuring and development of the coal industry
– SP6: Development of renewable energy
– SP7: Ensuring the implementation of the state programme.

The Action plan for the Year of the fight against cardiovascular diseases in Russia in 2015 was prepared by the Russian Ministry of Health in pursuance of the list of instructions of the President of Russia on the implementation of the Address to the Federal Assembly of December 4, 2014 ( No. Pr-2821 of December 5, 2014, subparagraph 13 of paragraph 1 ).

The plan provides for the implementation of scientific and practical measures in order to improve the qualifications of medical workers and the possibility of exchanging international experience on this issue.

Including, it is planned to organize a volunteer movement involving students from educational institutions of higher and secondary vocational education, aimed at promoting a healthy lifestyle and conducting measures to identify and prevent risk factors for the development of cardiovascular diseases.

In addition, thematic events will be held on the fight against cardiovascular diseases in the framework of the All-Russian educational forum "Seliger" and the International Youth Meeting "Tavrida". It is planned to hold mass physical culture events among various age groups aimed at promoting physical culture and sports. It is also planned to create schools for patients with cardiovascular diseases in medical organizations that provide primary health care, including using telemedicine technologies.

The measures included in the plan are aimed at improving the system of prophylaxis, diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular diseases, improving the system of medical rehabilitation, promoting a healthy lifestyle, and developing civil responsibility among the population for their own health and the health of their children.

The decisions taken will contribute to the coordination of activities and general methodological support for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular diseases, as well as the improvement of the medical rehabilitation system.

The government approved the Strategy for the development of export of services until 2025 (hereinafter - the Strategy) and a plan for its implementation.

The purpose of the Strategy is to create the prerequisites for increasing the competitiveness of Russian services in global markets and creating attractive conditions in Russia based on approaches to regulating and taxing export activities that are no less effective than competing jurisdictions.

The objectives of the Strategy: to determine the competitive potential and future directions for the development of Russian export of services by type of service, the formation of a systematic approach to removing barriers and problems in the field of export of services, the identification of priorities and tasks for supporting and expanding the export of services, motivating exporters.

The strategy is aimed at creating conditions for ensuring sustainable high growth rates of export of services in order to reach its volume of $ 100 billion per year by 2025.

The plan was developed taking into account proposals including regional executive authorities, public environmental organizations, and representatives of the business community.

The plan contains a set of measures at the federal, regional and inter-regional levels. The main directions of the plan implementation: standardization of environmental impact and transition to the best available technologies; specially protected natural territories and wildlife; Baikal natural territory; Arctic; climate; water; forest; environmental education.

The measures envisaged by the Plan are aimed at achieving the goals and objectives of the Fundamentals of state policy in the field of environmental development of the Russian Federation for the period up to 2030 (approved by the President of Russia on April 30, 2012) and the state program "Environmental Protection" for 2012–2020 (approved by government decree from April 15, 2014 No. 326).

The Federal Target Program "Development of the Republic of Karelia until 2020” aims at stimulating the development of the economic potential of the Republic of Karelia and its implementation, by increasing the competitiveness of basic and the creation of new industries and sectors of the economy infrastructure support for economic development, and development of social sphere.
